label: Routing as constrained graph search
lesson:
# Routing as constrained graph search

Routing turns a placed netlist into metal: every net's pins must be joined by wires and vias, with no shorts, no design-rule violations and no more wires through any region than it can hold. For a tool designer, routing is constrained graph search. Knowing exactly which graph, which constraint and which objective is what separates a router you can reason about from a pile of heuristics.

## The routing graph

A router models the layout as a graph $G = (V, E)$. In detailed routing, a vertex is a grid point on a routing track of one metal layer. Wire edges join neighbouring points along a track, and via edges join the same point on adjacent layers. Blockages (macros, power straps, pre-routed nets) delete vertices or edges. Each edge carries a cost: its length, plus extra for vias, wrong-way wiring or congestion.

Routing one two-pin net is then a shortest-path problem: on a grid with unit costs, breadth-first search (Lee's algorithm) solves it, and with general non-negative costs Dijkstra or A* does. A net with $k > 2$ pins needs a tree that may branch at points that are not pins. Finding the cheapest such tree is the Steiner tree problem in graphs, which is NP-hard, so routers decompose multipin nets into two-pin connections or build trees heuristically.

## Capacity couples the nets

If each net could use any edge, routing would split into independent searches. It cannot: a track segment holds one wire, and a gcell edge holds as many wires as it has tracks. This capacity constraint couples all nets. Formally, choose for each net $i$ a tree $T_i$ so that for every edge $e$, the number of trees using $e$ is at most $cap(e)$, and minimise $\sum_i cost(T_i)$.

Routing nets one at a time on shortest paths is a greedy heuristic for that problem. Early nets take the best tracks, later nets detour or fail, and a different order can succeed where this one failed. A failure under one order therefore says the instance is congested, not that it is infeasible. Rip-up and reroute and negotiated congestion exist to undo the damage of a bad order.

## Legality first, then cost

A routed layout is useful only if it can be manufactured, so legality is a constraint, not a cost: every net connected, no shorts, every spacing, width, area and via rule satisfied. Among legal routings, the objective is usually a weighted sum of wirelength and via count, with timing, crosstalk and yield terms for nets that need them. During search, rule violations are priced with penalties so the router can pass through a bad state on the way to a good one, but the final check is pass or fail.

Scale forces a decomposition. A modern block has millions of nets and billions of grid points, so production flows route coarsely first (global routing on gcells, a few thousand tracks folded into each edge) and then in detail inside the corridor each net was given. Pin locations come from placement, so routing quality is bounded by placement quality: a hot spot of pins creates congestion no router can remove.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters 5 to 7; Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation".

problems.q:
Routing one two-pin net on a grid with unit edge costs and blockages is which classical problem?

A) A shortest-path problem in a graph

B) A graph-coloring problem

C) A bipartite matching problem

D) A minimum-cut problem
problems.a: A shortest-path problem in a graph
problems.e: With one net and fixed costs the task is a single shortest path, which is why Lee's algorithm is breadth-first search and A* applies directly.

problems.q:
Which constraint turns routing many nets from a set of independent searches into a hard combinatorial problem?

A) Edge costs must be non-negative

B) Nets must be routed in alphabetical order

C) Each grid edge or track can be used by a limited number of nets

D) Each net must connect all its pins
problems.a: Each grid edge or track can be used by a limited number of nets
problems.e: Capacity couples the nets: one net's route consumes resources another needs. Without it each net is a separate shortest-path or Steiner problem.

problems.q:
Which constraint turns routing many nets from a set of independent searches into a hard combinatorial problem?

A) Nets must be routed in alphabetical order

B) Each grid edge or track can be used by a limited number of nets

C) Each net must connect all its pins

D) Edge costs must be non-negative
problems.a: Each grid edge or track can be used by a limited number of nets
problems.e: Capacity couples the nets: one net's route consumes resources another needs. Without it each net is a separate shortest-path or Steiner problem.

problems.q:
Why do routers treat design-rule correctness as a constraint rather than just another cost term?

A) A routing with any violation cannot be manufactured, however short it is

B) Violations never interact with wirelength

C) Design rules are cheap to compute

D) Costs must always be integers
problems.a: A routing with any violation cannot be manufactured, however short it is
problems.e: The output must be DRC-clean to be fabricated. Penalties steer the search, but the final check is pass or fail.

problems.q:
A router routes nets one at a time, each on its shortest path. Why can the result depend on the order?

A) Early nets consume tracks that later nets then have to detour around or cannot use

B) The first net's cost function is different

C) Shortest paths depend on the order of the edges in memory

D) Later nets are always routed on higher layers
problems.a: Early nets consume tracks that later nets then have to detour around or cannot use
problems.e: Sequential routing is greedy: earlier nets block later ones. That is the motivation for rip-up and reroute and for negotiation.

problems.q:
Why do routers treat design-rule correctness as a constraint rather than just another cost term?

A) Design rules are cheap to compute

B) Costs must always be integers

C) Violations never interact with wirelength

D) A routing with any violation cannot be manufactured, however short it is
problems.a: A routing with any violation cannot be manufactured, however short it is
problems.e: The output must be DRC-clean to be fabricated. Penalties steer the search, but the final check is pass or fail.

problems.q:
Why does routing quality depend heavily on placement?

A) Placement decides the via resistance

B) Placement writes the design rules

C) Placement chooses the metal layers

D) Placement fixes the pin locations and local pin density, which set wirelength and congestion before routing starts
problems.a: Placement fixes the pin locations and local pin density, which set wirelength and congestion before routing starts
problems.e: A router can only connect the pins where they are. A placement with a hot spot of pins creates congestion no router can remove.

problems.q:
A routing engine is asked to minimise total wirelength only. What is the main risk?

A) Via count drops too far

B) The router stops honouring pin locations

C) Nets crowd onto the shortest corridors and overflow them, causing detours or failure later

D) Timing always improves too much
problems.a: Nets crowd onto the shortest corridors and overflow them, causing detours or failure later
problems.e: Wirelength alone ignores capacity. Congestion-aware costs spread demand so that later nets and detailed routing still fit.

problems.q:
What does a gridded router gain by restricting wires to a track grid?

A) It makes every net the same length

B) It allows wires of any width without extra rules

C) Spacing between wires on different tracks is correct by construction, so checks become simple

D) It removes the need for vias
problems.a: Spacing between wires on different tracks is correct by construction, so checks become simple
problems.e: Tracks are placed at the legal pitch, so wires on distinct tracks satisfy the basic spacing rule automatically; only special rules remain to check.

label: Global versus detailed routing
lesson:
# Global versus detailed routing

Every production router splits the work in two. Global routing decides which coarse regions each net passes through, balancing demand against capacity over the whole chip. Detailed routing then draws exact wires and vias on tracks inside those regions, obeying every design rule. The split is what makes full-chip routing tractable, and the interface between the two stages is where many routability failures are born.

## What each stage decides

Global routing works on a coarse grid of gcells (global routing cells), each covering many tracks. Its graph has one vertex per gcell and an edge between adjacent gcells whose capacity is the number of usable tracks crossing their boundary. The output is, for each net, a set of gcells and layers: in OpenROAD these are written as route guides, rectangles per layer that bound where the net may go.

Detailed routing works on the full track grid inside those guides. It decides exact tracks, wire geometry, via positions and how each pin is reached, and it is responsible for DRC correctness: spacing, end-of-line, minimum area, via enclosure and the rest of the rule deck. Global routing reasons about resource allocation; detailed routing reasons about geometry.

## Why the coarse model can mislead

Gcell capacity is an estimate. It counts tracks crossing a boundary, but it cannot see that pins inside a gcell block some tracks, that a partial blockage cuts others, or that a detailed route needs local detours to reach a pin. So a global solution with zero overflow can still fail in detailed routing where pin density is high.

Flows defend against this in two ways. Layer adjustments shave a share of each layer's tracks off the capacity before global routing, leaving slack for detours and pin access. And the congestion map (overflow per edge) is read as a forecast: regions of high overflow are where detailed routing will struggle. Guides also trade flexibility for speed. A detailed router confined to its guides searches a small region and keeps global balance, but it cannot escape a guide that turns out to be locally blocked.

## Consequences for the flow

Placement estimates wirelength with half-perimeter bounds, a lower bound for each net in isolation. Global routing under capacity limits adds detours, so a large gap between placed and globally routed wirelength signals congestion. That is why routability-driven placement calls a fast global router or congestion estimate and spreads cells where it finds hot spots.

Runtime is dominated by detailed routing, which works on the fine grid and iterates search-and-repair until violations vanish. Gcell size is a real knob: halving it resolves local hot spots better but multiplies the vertex count by about four, and each edge then holds fewer tracks, so its capacity estimate becomes noisier.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the OpenROAD documentation for the grt and drt modules.

problems.q:

A) A coarse route through gcells (route guides), with no exact track positions

B) Exact polygons on every layer, ready for GDS

C) A placement of the net's driver

D) A timing report of the net
problems.a: A coarse route through gcells (route guides), with no exact track positions
problems.e: Global routing assigns each net to a sequence of gcells, which detailed routing then realises as exact wires on tracks.

problems.q:
Global routing reports zero overflow, but detailed routing fails in some regions. What is the likely cause?

A) The gcell capacity model overestimated usable tracks, for example by ignoring pin access or local blockages

B) Global routing used too few iterations

D) Zero overflow guarantees detailed routability, so the flow has a bug
problems.a: The gcell capacity model overestimated usable tracks, for example by ignoring pin access or local blockages

problems.q:

A) To reduce via count directly

B) To force every net onto the top layers

C) To make global routing run faster

problems.a: To leave slack for the detours and pin access that detailed routing will need
problems.e: Reserving a fraction of tracks keeps the coarse solution realistic about what detailed routing can achieve.

B) Global routing ignores multipin nets

C) Congestion forced detours that half-perimeter estimates cannot see

D) Detailed routing has already run

A) It assigns layers to cells

B) It skips global routing entirely

C) It routes clock nets first

D) It calls a fast global router or congestion estimate to find hot spots and spreads cells there

label: Routing grids, gcells and tracks
lesson:
# Routing grids, gcells and tracks

Before any search, a router builds its resource model: tracks on each layer and gcells that group them. The number of usable tracks crossing a gcell boundary becomes that edge's capacity in global routing, and every congestion number downstream is measured against it. Getting capacity right, including blockages and reserved slack, is the first computation in a routing engine.

## Tracks from pitch and offset

Each routing layer carries parallel tracks at a fixed pitch $p$, set by the layer's minimum width plus minimum spacing, starting from an offset $o$ given in the technology or DEF track definitions. Vertical tracks sit at $x = o + kp$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ A gcell column covering $[x_0, x_1)$ contains the tracks with $x_0 \le o + kp < x_1$, so the count is $\lfloor (x_1 - 1 - o)/p \rfloor - \lceil (x_0 - o)/p \rceil + 1$ for integer coordinates.

Example: $o = 70$ nm, $p = 140$ nm, gcell $[2800, 5600)$. The first track is at $k = \lceil 2730/140 \rceil = 20$ (x = 2870) and the last at $k = \lfloor 5529/140 \rfloor = 39$ (x = 5530), so the gcell holds 20 tracks. Gcells are usually sized to a fixed number of standard-cell row heights, so the track count per gcell differs from layer to layer.

## Blockages remove tracks

A macro, a power strap or a pre-routed wire makes some tracks unusable. A track is lost if a wire on it would violate spacing to the obstruction, that is, if its centerline lies within half the wire width plus the minimum spacing of the obstruction's edge. So a blockage over $[b_1, b_2]$ removes every track with $b_1 - m < x < b_2 + m$, where $m = w/2 + s$.

Example: tracks at $70 + 140k$ nm in a $[0, 2660)$ gcell (19 tracks), a blockage over $[1140, 1390]$ and $m = 35$ nm. The lost window is $(1105, 1425)$, which contains the tracks at 1190 and 1330, so the gcell keeps 17. Global routers compute these reductions per gcell edge and layer; a partial blockage reduces capacity proportionally rather than to zero.

## Capacity with reserved slack

The capacity of a gcell edge sums the usable tracks crossing it over all layers whose preferred direction runs across that boundary. Flows then reserve slack: a layer adjustment of 30% keeps only 70% of a layer's tracks, rounded down, leaving room for pin access, local detours and rules the coarse model cannot see. Lower layers usually get larger adjustments because pins crowd them.

Example: metal 2 has 10 tracks crossing an edge with a 40% adjustment, metal 4 has 13 with 60%. Capacity is $\lfloor 10 \cdot 0.6 \rfloor + \lfloor 13 \cdot 0.4 \rfloor = 6 + 5 = 11$. Too little adjustment and global routing reports a clean result that detailed routing cannot realise; too much and the global router detours nets for congestion that does not exist.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the LEF/DEF reference for TRACKS and GCELLGRID statements; the OpenROAD grt documentation on layer adjustments.

problems.q: Vertical routing tracks on a metal layer sit at x = 100 + 200k nm for k = 0, 1, 2, and so on. Gcells are 3520 nm wide, and gcell column 3 covers the half-open range [10560, 14080) nm. How many tracks of this layer run through that gcell column?

A track is unusable if its centerline lies strictly within 60 nm (half the wire width plus the minimum spacing) of the obstruction, that is, at 310 < x < 540. How many usable tracks does the gcell keep?

A track is unusable if its centerline lies strictly within 210 nm (half the wire width plus the minimum spacing) of the obstruction, that is, at 1900 < x < 3280. problems.q: A global router builds the capacity of a horizontal gcell edge from two horizontal layers. Metal 2 has 17 tracks crossing the edge and a layer adjustment of 50%; metal 4 has 16 tracks and an adjustment of 50%. The adjustment removes that share of the layer's tracks, and each layer's remaining capacity is rounded down to an integer. What capacity does the router assign to the edge?
problems.e: Metal 2 keeps floor(17 x 0.5) = 8 tracks and metal 4 keeps floor(16 x 0.5) = 8. The edge capacity is 16. Adjustments reserve room for pin access, power straps and detailed-routing detours that the gcell model cannot see.

problems.q: A global router builds the capacity of a horizontal gcell edge from two horizontal layers. Metal 2 has 18 tracks crossing the edge and a layer adjustment of 20%; metal 4 has 16 tracks and an adjustment of 60%. The adjustment removes that share of the layer's tracks, and each layer's remaining capacity is rounded down to an integer. What capacity does the router assign to the edge?
problems.e: Metal 2 keeps floor(18 x 0.8) = 14 tracks and metal 4 keeps floor(16 x 0.4) = 6. The edge capacity is 20. Adjustments reserve room for pin access, power straps and detailed-routing detours that the gcell model cannot see.

problems.q: A global router builds the capacity of a horizontal gcell edge from two horizontal layers. Metal 2 has 10 tracks crossing the edge and a layer adjustment of 50%; metal 4 has 20 tracks and an adjustment of 0%. The adjustment removes that share of the layer's tracks, and each layer's remaining capacity is rounded down to an integer. What capacity does the router assign to the edge?
problems.e: Metal 2 keeps floor(10 x 0.5) = 5 tracks and metal 4 keeps floor(20 x 1) = 20. The edge capacity is 25. Adjustments reserve room for pin access, power straps and detailed-routing detours that the gcell model cannot see.

label: Preferred directions and directional capacity
lesson:
# Preferred directions and directional capacity

Each metal layer has a preferred direction, and directions alternate up the stack. The convention keeps wires on one layer parallel, which simplifies spacing and lithography and makes track grids regular. It also means each bend in a route becomes a via, and each gcell edge draws its capacity only from the layers running across it. Directional capacity is the second half of the resource model.

## Directional capacity

If layer $M_i$ is horizontal, its tracks run east-west and carry wires across the boundaries between horizontally adjacent gcells. So the capacity of an east-west crossing is the sum of tracks over the horizontal routing layers only, and the capacity of a north-south crossing sums the vertical layers. Metal 1 is often reserved for cell-internal wiring and pins, so routing capacity starts at metal 2.

Example: a stack with M3, M5, M7 and M9 horizontal holding 13, 6, 12 and 5 tracks per gcell gives a horizontal edge capacity of 36. The vertical layers contribute nothing to that edge unless the router allows wrong-way wiring. Upper layers usually have wider pitch, hence fewer tracks, but lower resistance, which matters later for timing-driven layer assignment.

## Filling layers bottom-up

A simple layer assigner places wires on the lowest layer of the right direction first and moves up only when a layer is full. Low layers are close to the pins, so using them saves vias; high layers are reserved for long and critical nets. Given a demand of $D$ crossings and per-layer capacities $c_1, c_2, \dots$ for the horizontal layers in order, the highest layer used is the first $k$ with $c_1 + \dots + c_k \ge D$.

Example: horizontal layers M3 with 8 tracks and M5 with 14. A demand of 22 crossings fills M3 and needs all 14 of M5, so M5 is the highest layer used. If the demand exceeds the total over all horizontal layers, the edge overflows no matter how layers are assigned, which is why global routing can work on the 2D projection with summed capacities.

## Wrong-way wiring

Some routers allow short wires against a layer's preferred direction, at a cost. A wrong-way step uses a track that crosses other tracks of the same layer, so it blocks several of them; routers charge a multiple $f > 1$ of the normal step cost. The alternative to a wrong-way jog of $n$ steps is a via down to a layer of the other direction, $n$ normal steps and a via back up.

With step cost 1, via cost $c_v$ and wrong-way factor $f$, the jog is cheaper when $fn < n + 2c_v$, that is $n < 2c_v/(f - 1)$. With $c_v = 4$ and $f = 3$ the bound is 4, so jogs of up to 3 steps stay on the layer. Advanced nodes often forbid wrong-way wiring on the lowest layers entirely, because their patterning only prints lines in one direction.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), on routing grids and layer stacks.

problems.q: A stack has metal layers M1 to M7 with alternating preferred directions, M1 being vertical. M1 is reserved for cell pins, so routing uses M2 and above: M2 horizontal with 8 tracks per gcell; M3 vertical with 13 tracks per gcell; M4 horizontal with 11 tracks per gcell; M5 vertical with 9 tracks per gcell; M6 horizontal with 4 tracks per gcell; M7 vertical with 8 tracks per gcell. Wires crossing the boundary between two horizontally adjacent gcells run east-west. What is the capacity of that boundary, in tracks, counting every routing layer that can carry such wires in its preferred direction?
problems.e: An east-west crossing uses horizontal tracks, so only the horizontal layers M2, M4, M6 count. Their tracks sum to 23. Vertical layers contribute nothing to this edge unless the router allows wrong-way wiring.

problems.q: A detailed router charges 1 per track step in a layer's preferred direction and 3 per step against it (wrong-way), and 6 per via. A net on a horizontal layer needs a short vertical jog of n steps. It can jog wrong-way on the same layer, or drop a via to the vertical layer below, run n preferred-direction steps and via back up. What is the largest n for which the wrong-way jog is strictly cheaper?
problems.e: Wrong-way costs 3n; the via detour costs n + 2(6). The jog wins when 3n < n + 12, that is n < 6, so the largest integer is 5.

problems.q: A detailed router charges 1 per track step in a layer's preferred direction and 2 per step against it (wrong-way), and 7 per via. A net on a horizontal layer needs a short vertical jog of n steps. It can jog wrong-way on the same layer, or drop a via to the vertical layer below, run n preferred-direction steps and via back up. What is the largest n for which the wrong-way jog is strictly cheaper?
problems.e: Wrong-way costs 2n; the via detour costs n + 2(7). The jog wins when 2n < n + 14, that is n < 14, so the largest integer is 13.

problems.e: Wrong-way costs 2.5n; the via detour costs n + 2(4). The jog wins when 2.5n < n + 8, that is n < 5.333, so the largest integer is 5.

label: The global-routing grid graph
lesson:
# The global-routing grid graph

The global router's data structure is a grid graph over gcells, in 2D with summed capacities or in 3D with one copy per layer joined by vias. Its size sets memory and runtime, its edges carry capacity and demand, and blockages are expressed by lowering edge capacities. Counting its parts precisely is how a tool designer sizes arrays and estimates cost before writing a line of search code.

## The 2D gcell graph

Tile the die into $X$ columns and $Y$ rows of gcells. The 2D graph has $XY$ vertices, $(X-1)Y$ horizontal edges and $X(Y-1)$ vertical edges. Each edge stores a capacity (summed over the layers of its direction), a demand (wires currently routed across it) and, during negotiation, a history cost.

Example: a 17 by 102 gcell grid has $16 \cdot 102 = 1632$ horizontal and $17 \cdot 101 = 1717$ vertical edges, 3349 in all. A large block may have a grid of thousands by thousands of gcells, so edges number in the millions, and per-edge storage is a few integers. Routers store edges in arrays indexed by position rather than as an adjacency list, because the grid is regular.

## The 3D graph with layers

A 3D global-routing graph keeps one grid per layer. Because each layer has a preferred direction, a horizontal layer has only the $(X-1)Y$ horizontal edges and a vertical layer only the $X(Y-1)$ vertical ones. Via edges join each gcell to the same gcell on the next layer: $(L-1)XY$ via edges for $L$ layers.

Example: $41 \times 16$ gcells on 4 layers, the lowest vertical. Two vertical layers give $2 \cdot 41 \cdot 15 = 1230$ wire edges, two horizontal layers $2 \cdot 40 \cdot 16 = 1280$, and three via levels $3 \cdot 656 = 1968$, so 4478 edges. Via edges usually carry a capacity too, since too many vias in one gcell block tracks on every layer they cross. Many global routers route on the 2D projection and assign layers afterwards because the 2D graph is $L$ times smaller.

## Blockages on the graph

A macro covering an $a \times b$ block of gcells lowers the capacity of every edge it touches, typically to zero on the layers it blocks. Inside the block there are $(a-1)b + a(b-1)$ edges, and if the block sits away from the die edge, $2a + 2b$ more edges cross its boundary. Both sets must be updated, because a wire crossing the boundary needs tracks inside the macro's first gcell.

Example: an 11 by 12 macro touches $10 \cdot 12 + 11 \cdot 11 = 241$ internal edges and $2 \cdot 11 + 2 \cdot 12 = 46$ boundary edges, 287 in all. A partial obstruction instead scales capacity by the fraction of tracks it blocks. Getting this wrong in either direction shows up later as phantom congestion or as overflow the global router never saw.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the FastRoute papers by Pan and Chu for 2D global routing with later layer assignment.

label: Lee's maze router
lesson:
# Lee's maze router

Lee's algorithm (1961) is the founding maze router: breadth-first search on the routing grid, phrased as a wavefront that floods outward from the source until it reaches the target. It is guaranteed to find a shortest route if one exists. Every later maze router, from Hadlock's to A*, is a way to get Lee's guarantee while expanding fewer cells or using less memory.

## Wavefront expansion

Label the source 0. Every free neighbour of a cell labelled $k$ that has no label yet receives $k + 1$. The cells labelled $k$ form the $k$-th wavefront, and they are exactly the cells at shortest-route distance $k$ from the source, because blockages are simply never labelled and the wave flows around them. The search stops when the target receives a label $D$, the length of the shortest route in grid steps.

If the Manhattan distance between the pins is 6 but a wall forces the route around one end, the target might receive label 8. The cost of the method is the expansion: with unit costs Lee processes each reachable cell once, $O(N)$ for $N$ grid cells. It is complete (it finds a route whenever one exists) and optimal for unit edge costs.

## How many cells the wave touches

Lee stops as soon as the target is labelled, but by then every cell with a smaller label has been labelled too. So the work is at least the number of reachable cells with label below $D$. On an open grid that number grows like the area of a diamond of radius $D$, about $2D^2$ cells, while the route itself has only $D$ steps. Most of the labelled cells lie behind the source or off to the side, nowhere near the target.

Example: on a 6 by 6 grid with a wall, a target at label 8 might be reached only after 20 cells with labels 0 to 7 have been labelled. This waste is what Hadlock's detour ordering and A*'s heuristic attack, and it is why practical routers bound the search to a box around the pins.

## Label memory

A naive implementation stores the full label in every cell. A label can reach the number of cells minus 1, and two more codes are needed for empty and blocked, so a grid of $N$ cells needs $\lceil \log_2 (N + 2) \rceil$ bits per cell: 23 bits for a 2100 by 2400 grid, about 116 million bits in all.

The backtrace only needs to recognise a cell's predecessor, whose label is one less. Storing labels modulo 3 (sequence 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3) suffices, because a cell's neighbours on shortest routes carry labels $k-1$, $k$ or $k+1$, which are distinct mod 3. With empty and blocked that is 5 codes, 3 bits. Akers' coding (sequence 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1) needs only two label values, so 4 codes fit in 2 bits per cell. Memory dropped by an order of magnitude with no loss of optimality.

## Going deeper

C. Y. Lee, "An Algorithm for Path Connections and Its Applications" (1961); S. B. Akers, "A Modification of Lee's Path Connection Algorithm" (1967); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Backtrace and path choice in Lee routing
lesson:
# Backtrace and path choice in Lee routing

Wavefront labels tell you how far each cell is from the source, but not which route to take. The backtrace recovers a route by walking from the target down the labels. Usually many shortest routes exist, and the choice among them decides bends, vias and congestion. A good backtrace policy is a cheap way to get a better route from the same search.

## Walking down the labels

Start at the target with label $D$. Step to any neighbour labelled $D - 1$, then to a neighbour of that cell labelled $D - 2$, and so on until the source (label 0). Each step lowers the label by exactly one, so the route has exactly $D$ steps and is shortest. The backtrace never needs to search: at every cell at least one neighbour carries the next lower label, because that is how the cell received its own.

The number of choices at the first step is the number of target neighbours labelled $D - 1$. If it is more than one, the router needs a tie-breaking rule. Once the route is found, its cells are marked as used (blocked for the next net) and all other labels are cleared.

## Counting shortest routes

The set of shortest routes forms a directed acyclic graph: an edge from $u$ to $v$ whenever $v$ is a neighbour of $u$ with label one higher. The number of shortest routes to a cell is the sum of the counts of its neighbours with label one less, starting from 1 at the source. Process cells wavefront by wavefront and the count at the target is the number of distinct shortest routes.

On an open grid between pins $d_x$ columns and $d_y$ rows apart this gives the lattice-path count $\binom{d_x + d_y}{d_x}$. Blockages cut it down sharply: behind a wall with a single gap, every shortest route squeezes through the gap, and the count becomes a product of the counts on each side. A large count means freedom, which the backtrace can spend on fewer bends or on avoiding congested cells.

## Tie-breaking for fewer bends

Among shortest routes, a router prefers the one with the fewest bends, because in a preferred-direction stack every bend needs a via. A simple policy keeps the current direction whenever a neighbour in that direction has the next lower label. That greedy rule is not always optimal; the exact minimum comes from dynamic programming over (cell, incoming direction) states on the shortest-route DAG, adding 1 whenever the direction changes.

Example: if the target is reached through a gap in a wall, the best shortest route may need 2 bends (go to the gap's row, cross, turn toward the target), while a careless backtrace zigzags with 5. Tie-breaking costs nothing in search effort, which is why routers add direction and congestion preferences to the backtrace before they reach for heavier tools.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation", on maze routing.

label: Hadlock's minimum-detour router
lesson:
# Hadlock's minimum-detour router

Hadlock's router (1977) keeps Lee's guarantee of a shortest route but changes the order of search. Instead of labelling cells by distance from the source, it labels them by detour number: how many moves away from the target a route needed to reach them. Search proceeds in order of detours, so it pushes straight at the target and spreads sideways only when blocked.

## Counting detours

A move is a detour if it increases the Manhattan distance to the target. Each detour must later be undone by an extra move toward the target, so a route of length $l$ between pins at Manhattan distance $MD$ with $d$ detours satisfies $l = MD + 2d$. The detour count of a route is therefore $d = (l - MD)/2$, however the detours are interleaved.

Example: from (1, 2) to (5, 6) the Manhattan distance is 8. A route of 12 moves, say E E W E W E N E N N E N, makes $(12 - 8)/2 = 2$ detours: the two W moves. Minimising length and minimising detours are the same objective, which is why Hadlock's router is still optimal.

## Expanding by detour number

Hadlock labels each cell with the fewest detours on any route from the source to it, and expands cells in order of that label. A move toward the target keeps the label; a move away increases it by 1. So the search first floods every cell reachable with zero detours, then with one, and so on, until the target is reached. The label of the target is the minimum detour number $d^*$, and the route length is $MD + 2d^*$.

Example: the shortest route around a wall is 11 steps long between pins 3 apart. The minimum detour number is $(11 - 3)/2 = 4$. A cell's Hadlock label is $(dist(s, v) - MD(s, t) + MD(v, t))/2$, where $dist(s, v)$ is its shortest-route distance from the source. This shows the labels are just Lee distances corrected by progress toward the target.

## Why it expands less

With no obstacles, every cell inside the pins' bounding box is reachable with zero detours, and nothing outside it is, so Hadlock expands only the box while Lee floods a diamond of radius $MD$ around the source. Obstacles add detours only where needed. The labels are small integers that grow slowly, which keeps the priority structure simple (a list per detour level).

The price is that the target's position must be known up front, so the method suits two-pin connections; multipin nets are decomposed first. Hadlock is an early instance of goal-directed search: in A* terms, it is Dijkstra on the reduced cost $l - (MD(s,t) - MD(v,t))$, which is exactly twice the detour count.

## Going deeper

F. O. Hadlock, "A Shortest Path Algorithm for Grid Graphs" (1977); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Soukup's fast maze router
lesson:
# Soukup's fast maze router

Soukup's router (1978) takes a different trade: it gives up the guarantee of a shortest route to gain speed. It walks greedily toward the target and falls back to breadth-first expansion only when it is blocked. On typical layouts with long open stretches it touches far fewer cells than Lee, and it still finds a route whenever one exists.

## Greedy first, breadth-first when blocked

From the current cell, Soukup's router moves in the direction of the target, depth-first, without branching. When the straight move is blocked, it switches to breadth-first expansion from the cells reached so far until it finds a cell from which it can again move toward the target, and then resumes the greedy walk. The search alternates between these two modes until the target is reached.

On an open grid between pins at Manhattan distance $d$, the greedy phase alone reaches the target after about $d$ cells. Lee would label on the order of $d^2$ cells in the same situation. The breadth-first fallback is what keeps the method complete: if a route exists, the expansion eventually finds a way around every wall.

## What is guaranteed and what is not

Soukup's router always finds a route if one exists, but not necessarily a shortest one. The greedy walk can commit to the wrong side of an obstacle and then detour around it, producing a route longer than Lee's or Hadlock's. Hadlock, by contrast, also speeds up Lee but preserves optimality by ordering search by detours.

A ranking of search effort on a lightly blocked grid is usually Soukup fewest, then Hadlock, then Lee. In a dense maze of obstacles the greedy moves keep failing and Soukup's advantage shrinks toward Lee's behaviour. For non-critical nets a somewhat longer route costs little, and the runtime saved across millions of nets is the point.

## Where the idea went

The core idea, biasing the search toward the target so open space is crossed with little expansion, survives in every modern detailed router. What replaced Soukup's specific procedure is A*: a priority search with an admissible, consistent heuristic gets most of the same speedup while keeping optimality, and it handles general edge costs (vias, bends, congestion) that a pure greedy walk cannot weigh.

So a reviewer should object if a router uses Soukup-style search for timing-critical nets, where extra length costs delay. For bulk nets in open regions, a fast incomplete-optimality search is a legitimate engineering choice, as long as the router can rip up and reroute what it gets wrong.

## Going deeper

J. Soukup, "Fast Maze Router" (1978); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: A* routing
lesson:
# A* routing

A* is the maze search used inside modern detailed and global routers. It expands cells in order of $f = g + h$, the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go. With the Manhattan distance as $h$ on a unit-cost grid, the estimate never overshoots, so A* still finds a shortest route while expanding far fewer cells than Lee's wavefront.

## Priority f equals g plus h

For a cell $v$, $g(v)$ is the cost of the best route found from the source to $v$, and $h(v)$ estimates the remaining cost to the target. A* keeps an open list ordered by $f(v) = g(v) + h(v)$ and always expands the smallest. On a grid with unit step cost the Manhattan distance $h(v) = |x_v - x_t| + |y_v - y_t|$ is admissible (it never exceeds the true remaining cost) and consistent ($h(u) \le 1 + h(v)$ for neighbours), so A* returns a shortest route.

Example: a cell reached by its shortest route of length $g = 8$ that is 5 columns and rows from the target has $f = 13$. If the best route to the target costs 12, that cell will never be expanded by a correct A*, while Lee would label it.

## Cells A* must expand

Let $C^*$ be the cost of the best route. With a consistent heuristic, $f$ never decreases along a shortest route, and A* expands every cell with $f(v) < C^*$ before it finishes; cells with $f(v) = C^*$ may or may not be expanded, depending on tie-breaking, and cells with $f(v) > C^*$ never are. Lee, by contrast, must label every reachable cell with $g(v) < C^*$.

So the guaranteed saving is the count of cells with $g < C^*$ minus the count with $f < C^*$. Example: with $C^* = 9$, Lee must label 24 cells while A* must expand only 10. The cells pruned are those whose Manhattan distance to the target makes them hopeless. On an open grid every cell in the pins' bounding box has $f = C^*$, so A* with good tie-breaking (prefer larger $g$) walks almost straight to the target.

## Heuristics with real costs

Real routers price vias, bends, wrong-way steps and congestion, so step costs are not all 1. The heuristic must stay admissible under those costs: Manhattan distance times the cheapest per-step cost, plus the minimum number of vias the target still needs times the via cost, is a common choice. An inadmissible heuristic (for example, weighting $h$ by more than 1) searches faster but may return a longer route; some routers accept that trade for non-critical nets.

A* also needs a clean priority queue, and on large grids the open and closed sets dominate memory. Detailed routers bound the search to the net's route guides or a box around the pins, which caps both. The search must also handle many sources and targets at once (a partial tree, a pin shape with several access points), which A* does by seeding all sources with $g = 0$ and using the distance to the nearest target as $h$.

## Going deeper

Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, "A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths" (1968); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the TritonRoute papers for A* in detailed routing.

label: Bend and via costs in maze routing
lesson:
# Bend and via costs in maze routing

Shortest is not the same as best. In a stack where each layer carries one direction, every bend in a route forces a via, and vias add resistance, block tracks on the layers they cross and reduce yield. Routers therefore price bends and vias explicitly, which changes both the search state and the routes it finds.

## Pricing a route

A route's cost is the sum of its step costs plus a penalty per bend or via: $cost = L + b \cdot B$ for length $L$, bend count $B$ and bend cost $b$, with more terms for wrong-way steps or congested edges. In a preferred-direction stack a bend in the plane is a layer change, so bend cost and via cost are the same thing seen from 2D.

Example: moves N N N N E E E N N N N E E E N have length 15 and change direction 4 times. With a bend cost of 6 the route costs $15 + 24 = 39$. A route with one more step and two fewer bends would cost $16 + 12 = 28$, so the longer route wins. The bend penalty encodes the router's real preference for straight wires.

## Direction-aware search

A bend cost depends on the direction a route arrives from, so a search on cells alone cannot price it. The router searches over states (cell, incoming direction): moving in the same direction costs one step, turning costs one step plus the bend cost. Dijkstra or A* on this expanded graph, four states per cell on a 2D grid, finds the exact cheapest route.

Example: on a grid where the shortest route has 9 steps and 4 bends and another has 11 steps and 2 bends, a bend cost of 4 gives $9 + 16 = 25$ against $11 + 8 = 19$, so the search returns the longer, straighter route at cost 19 (or something cheaper still if it exists). In 3D the state is simply the (cell, layer) vertex, and the via edge carries the cost; the effect is the same.

## When a longer route wins

Two candidates make the trade explicit. Route A is $L_A$ steps with $k_A$ vias, route B is $L_B > L_A$ steps with $k_B < k_A$ vias. With step cost 1 and via cost $v$, B is cheaper when $L_B + k_B v < L_A + k_A v$, that is $v > (L_B - L_A)/(k_A - k_B)$.

Example: A is 11 steps with 5 vias, B is 21 steps with 4 vias. B wins only when $v > 10$, so at any realistic via cost the short route stays. Choosing the via cost is a policy decision: too low and routes zigzag through via stacks that hurt resistance and yield; too high and nets take long detours that add capacitance and congestion. It is exactly the kind of knob that belongs in a router's parameters rather than its core.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Line-probe routing
prereqs: Backtrace and path choice in Lee routing
lesson:
# Line-probe routing

Line-probe routers, by Mikami and Tabuchi (1968) and Hightower (1969), search with straight lines instead of cells. They shoot escape lines from the pins, then perpendicular lines from points on those, until a line from the source meets a line from the target. They store a few segments instead of a label per cell, and the routes they find have few bends.

## Minimum bends

Mikami-Tabuchi starts with level-0 lines: from each pin, straight lines in all four directions until they hit a blockage or the grid edge. At level $i + 1$ it launches perpendicular lines from every grid point of the level-$i$ lines. The search stops when a source line intersects a target line. Every level adds one bend, so the first intersection gives a route with the fewest possible bends, which is also the fewest straight segments.

Example: if the target sits behind a wall with a gap, the route might need 3 bends: out of the source, into the gap's row, through, and down to the target. The route is not necessarily shortest in length, but in a preferred-direction stack fewer bends mean fewer vias.

## Probe lines and what they cover

A level-0 line runs from the pin until the first blocked cell or the grid edge. The cells on the four level-0 lines of the source are exactly the cells reachable with zero bends. The cells reachable with at most one bend are those on the level-0 lines plus every cell on a perpendicular line launched from them.

Example: a source in an open corner might cover 8 cells with its level-0 lines and 15 with one bend. A line-probe router stores each line as a segment (two endpoints), so memory scales with the number of lines rather than with the area of the grid. Hightower's variant is greedier: it launches only a few lines from carefully chosen escape points, which is faster but can fail to find a route that exists.

## Line probing versus maze routing

Maze routers label cells and guarantee shortest routes; line probers store segments and aim for few bends. Mikami-Tabuchi is complete (it finds a route if one exists) because every grid point of every line launches the next level. Hightower trades completeness for speed. Neither handles general edge costs as naturally as a priority search.

In practice, line-probe ideas survive in gridless detailed routers and in fast connection searches through open areas, often followed by a maze search when the probes fail. Because each line is a segment, the representation pairs well with interval and corner-stitched data structures. The fewest-bend property also matches what a preferred-direction router wants: long straight runs with few layer changes.

## Going deeper

K. Mikami and K. Tabuchi, "A Computer Program for Optimal Routing of Printed Circuit Conductors" (1968); D. W. Hightower, "A Solution to Line-Routing Problems on the Continuous Plane" (1969); Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation".

label: Pattern routing
lesson:
# Pattern routing

Maze search is too slow to run on every net of a million-net design. Pattern routing instead tries a handful of predefined shapes for each two-pin connection: the two L shapes with one bend, and the Z shapes with two. Most nets route well this way, and only the leftovers need maze search. Global routers such as FastRoute start every net with patterns.

## Counting Z shapes

Take a two-pin connection whose pins are $d_x \ge 2$ columns and $d_y \ge 2$ rows apart on the gcell grid. A Z shape is a monotone route with exactly two bends. An HVH Z runs horizontally, jogs vertically at some column strictly between the pins, then continues horizontally; there are $d_x - 1$ such columns. A VHV Z jogs horizontally at a row strictly between the pins; there are $d_y - 1$.

So the pattern router considers $(d_x - 1) + (d_y - 1) = d_x + d_y - 2$ Z shapes. Example: pins at (16, 13) and (22, 16) give $5 + 2 = 7$ Z shapes. A jog at a pin's own column would just be an L shape, which is why the jog must be strictly inside.

## All pattern candidates

An L shape has one bend: horizontal then vertical, or vertical then horizontal. When the pins differ in both coordinates there are exactly 2. Together with the Z shapes a pattern router evaluates $2 + (d_x + d_y - 2) = d_x + d_y$ candidates per connection, linear in the distance between the pins.

Each candidate's cost is the sum of the costs of the gcell edges it crosses, plus a bend or via penalty. Computing a cost takes time proportional to the route length, and prefix sums along rows and columns cut that to constant time per candidate. A net in a single row or column has only its straight route. The router picks the cheapest candidate, adds its demand to the edges, and moves on.

## What patterns miss

A monotone route never moves away from the target, and there are $\binom{d_x + d_y}{d_x}$ of them, the lattice-path count. Patterns cover only $d_x + d_y$ of these. Example: for $d_x = 2$, $d_y = 6$ there are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ monotone routes, of which 2 are L shapes and 6 are Z shapes, so 20 staircase routes with three or more bends are never considered.

That is the trade: patterns are fast and produce few vias, but in a congested region the best route may be a staircase or may need a detour outside the bounding box. Global routers therefore escalate: L and Z first, then monotonic routing by dynamic programming over all staircases, then full maze routing with detours for what is still overflowed. FastRoute later added three-bend patterns as an intermediate step.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); M. Pan and C. Chu, "FastRoute: A Step to Integrate Global Routing into Placement" (2006).

label: Choosing patterns on a congestion map
lesson:
# Choosing patterns on a congestion map

A pattern router does not ask which shape is shortest; all monotone shapes have the same length. It asks which is cheapest on the current congestion map, where each gcell edge's cost rises as its demand approaches capacity. Evaluating patterns against that map, with a penalty for bends, is the inner loop of fast global routing.

## The cheaper L

Place the pins at gcells $(0, 0)$ and $(d_x, d_y)$. Let $h_{y,x}$ be the cost of the horizontal edge from $(x, y)$ to $(x+1, y)$ and $v_{x,y}$ the cost of the vertical edge from $(x, y)$ to $(x, y+1)$. The horizontal-first L costs the row-0 edges plus the column-$d_x$ edges; the vertical-first L costs the column-0 edges plus the row-$d_y$ edges.

Example: pins at (0, 0) and (2, 1); row 0 costs 3 and 9, column 2 costs 8, so HV costs 20; column 0 costs 8 and row 1 costs 1 and 9, so VH costs 18. The router picks VH at 18. Only the boundary rows and columns of the bounding box matter for L shapes, which is what makes them so cheap to evaluate.

## Adding Z shapes

An HVH Z with its jog at column $j$ costs row 0 from 0 to $j$, column $j$ from 0 to $d_y$, and row $d_y$ from $j$ to $d_x$. A VHV Z with its jog at row $i$ costs column 0 up to $i$, row $i$ across, and column $d_x$ from $i$ up. The router evaluates every jog position and keeps the cheapest pattern overall.

With prefix sums along each row and column, each Z costs three lookups, so all $d_x + d_y$ patterns are evaluated in linear time. The Z shapes let a route slip through a cheap column or row in the middle of the box while still avoiding expensive edges at the boundary. On a map where both L shapes cross a hot spot, a Z often wins at the price of one extra bend.

## Bends as a cost

Each bend becomes a via after layer assignment, so pattern routers add a penalty $b$ per bend: an L costs its edges plus $b$, a Z its edges plus $2b$. A cheap Z can then lose to a slightly more expensive L.

Example: the best L costs 7 in edges and the best Z costs 18; with $b = 2$ the L costs 9 and the Z 22. With edge costs closer together, say L at 14 and Z at 11, a penalty of $b = 4$ flips the choice to the L (18 against 19). The bend penalty is a policy knob: it trades congestion relief against via count, and its right value depends on the stack and on how expensive vias are in yield and resistance.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the FastRoute papers by Pan and Chu.

label: Monotonic routing by dynamic programming
prereqs: Choosing patterns on a congestion map
lesson:
# Monotonic routing by dynamic programming

Monotonic routing searches every route that never moves away from the target, not just the L and Z shapes. Because such routes form a directed acyclic grid, dynamic programming finds the cheapest one in time linear in the area of the bounding box. FastRoute 2.0 introduced it as the step between pattern routing and full maze routing.

## The dynamic program

Place the source at $(0, 0)$ and the target at $(d_x, d_y)$. Let $B(x, y)$ be the cheapest monotone cost from the source to gcell $(x, y)$. Then $B(0, 0) = 0$ and
$$B(x, y) = \min\big(B(x-1, y) + h_{y, x-1},\ B(x, y-1) + v_{x, y-1}\big),$$
taking only the terms that exist on the box boundary. Fill the table row by row; $B(d_x, d_y)$ is the answer.

Example: in a 3 by 3 box of gcells the table has 9 entries and each takes one comparison. The route itself is recovered by remembering which term won at each entry. This is the same principle of optimality that underlies shortest paths on a DAG: every monotone route to $(x, y)$ arrives from the west or from the south.

## Scaling to larger boxes

The work is one constant-time update per gcell in the bounding box, $(d_x + 1)(d_y + 1)$ in all, against $\binom{d_x + d_y}{d_x}$ routes enumerated explicitly. For a 4 by 3 box that is 20 table entries against 35 routes; for a 20 by 20 box it is 441 entries against more than $10^{11}$ routes.

Pins can be in any relative position: the router reflects the coordinates so the target is to the north-east, or runs the recurrence in the matching directions. Edge costs come from the current congestion map, so the program is re-run whenever a net is ripped up. Because it never leaves the bounding box, monotonic routing cannot detour around a fully blocked box; that case needs maze routing.

## Monotone versus patterns

Every L and Z shape is monotone, so the best monotone route costs at most the best pattern. The difference is what the extra flexibility buys: a staircase can thread around several expensive edges that every pattern must cross. Example: on a 4 by 3 map, the best pattern might cost 30 while the best monotone route costs 23, a saving of 7.

The cost is more bends. A staircase can turn at every gcell, and every turn is a potential via, so routers either add a bend penalty to the recurrence (which needs the incoming direction in the state, doubling the table) or accept monotone routes only where patterns leave overflow. In the escalation from patterns to monotone to maze, each stage is applied only to the nets the previous stage could not route cleanly.

## Going deeper

M. Pan and C. Chu, "FastRoute 2.0: A High-quality and Efficient Global Router" (2007); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Decomposing multipin nets into two-pin nets
prereqs: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
lesson:
# Decomposing multipin nets into two-pin nets

Routers search for paths between two points, but most nets have more pins. Global routers therefore decompose each multipin net into two-pin connections, usually along a rectilinear Steiner or spanning tree, and route those. The choice of decomposition fixes how much demand the net places on the grid before any search starts.

## Spanning-tree decomposition

Build a rectilinear minimum spanning tree over the pins with Manhattan distances: Prim's algorithm adds, at each step, the outside pin closest to any pin already in the tree. Its $n - 1$ edges become the two-pin connections. Example: pins at (5, 15), (4, 4), (17, 9) and (7, 5) give an MST of length 30, and each of its 3 edges is routed separately (by patterns, then maze if needed).

MST decomposition is simple and deterministic, but it never uses Steiner points, places where a tree branches away from a pin. On a rectilinear grid that costs wire: the MST can be up to 1.5 times as long as the optimal Steiner tree (Hwang's bound). Global routers usually start from a Steiner tree instead.

## Steiner points save wire

For three pins the optimal rectilinear Steiner tree is easy: put one Steiner point at the median x and median y of the pins and connect each pin to it. Its length equals the half-perimeter of the pins' bounding box, which is optimal for three pins. Then decompose into three two-pin connections, each from a pin to the Steiner point.

Example: pins at (0, 0), (10, 2) and (4, 9). The MST is $12 + 13 = 25$; the Steiner point is (4, 2) and the tree has length $10 + 9 = 19$, the half-perimeter, saving 6. For more pins the problem is NP-hard, and routers use fast heuristics or lookup methods such as FLUTE that are optimal or near optimal for small degrees.

## Why not a star from the driver

A naive decomposition connects the driver to every sink directly. Its total length is $\sum_i d(s, t_i)$, often far more than an MST, because sinks close to each other each get their own long wire back to the driver. Example: a driver at one corner and four sinks clustered at the opposite corner pays the long distance four times.

The star's one virtue is that every sink gets a shortest path from the driver, which minimises source-to-sink delay when wire resistance dominates. That trade between total wirelength and source-to-sink path length is exactly what timing-driven tree construction (Prim-Dijkstra trade-offs) controls. For ordinary nets, total length is what loads the routing grid, so Steiner or spanning decompositions win.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); F. K. Hwang, "On Steiner Minimal Trees with Rectilinear Distance" (1976).

label: FLUTE lookup-table Steiner trees
prereqs: Decomposing multipin nets into two-pin nets
lesson:
# FLUTE lookup-table Steiner trees

FLUTE (Chu and Wong) builds rectilinear Steiner minimal trees by table lookup. For low-degree nets, which dominate real designs, it is optimal and runs in time comparable to computing a bounding box. Nearly every academic and open-source global router, including FastRoute and OpenROAD's grt, starts its net topologies from FLUTE.

## Position sequences

Sort a net's $n$ pins by x coordinate, and record for each pin the rank of its y coordinate. The resulting permutation of $1, \dots, n$ is the net's position sequence. Two nets with the same sequence have the same relative arrangement of pins, so they share the same family of candidate optimal topologies, regardless of the actual distances.

There are $n!$ possible sequences: 24 for degree 4, 720 for degree 6, 40320 for degree 8. FLUTE precomputes a table entry for each sequence of low degree (the published tables cover degrees up to 9, with symmetries reducing storage). Larger nets are broken recursively into smaller ones that the table covers, at a small cost in optimality.

## Wirelength vectors

Let $h_1, \dots, h_{n-1}$ be the gaps between adjacent distinct x coordinates of the pins and $v_1, \dots, v_{n-1}$ the gaps between adjacent y coordinates. Any rectilinear Steiner tree on the Hanan grid has a length $\sum a_i h_i + \sum b_i v_i$ with small non-negative integer coefficients. FLUTE's table stores, for each sequence, only the coefficient vectors that can be optimal for some gaps: the potentially optimal wirelength vectors.

At query time FLUTE computes the gaps, evaluates each stored vector and returns the minimum. Example: for a degree-4 sequence with vectors (1, 1, 1 | 1, 2, 1) and (1, 2, 1 | 1, 1, 1) and gaps h = (5, 8, 3), v = (3, 9, 6), the values are 43 and 42, so the tree length is 42, the half-perimeter 34 plus the smaller middle gap 8.

## FLUTE inside a global router

FLUTE optimises wirelength only. It knows nothing about congestion, so a global router treats its tree as a starting topology. FastRoute, for example, constructs congestion-driven Steiner trees by shifting tree edges and Steiner points toward less congested gcells, then decomposes the tree into two-pin connections for pattern and maze routing.

The design lesson is the split between a fast, exact-enough geometric kernel and a cost-aware policy layered on top. FLUTE is a pure function from pin coordinates to a tree, deterministic and cacheable, which is exactly what a router wants in its inner loop. Its accuracy is excellent for the low degrees where it is exact and degrades slowly for large nets because of net breaking.

## Going deeper

C. Chu and Y.-C. Wong, "FLUTE: Fast Lookup Table Based Rectilinear Steiner Minimal Tree Algorithm for VLSI Design" (IEEE TCAD, 2008); M. Pan and C. Chu, "FastRoute" papers.

label: Routing congestion and overflow
lesson:
# Routing congestion and overflow

Congestion is the language of global routing. Every gcell edge has a capacity (usable tracks) and a demand (wires routed across it), and overflow is the excess. Total overflow, maximum overflow and the count of overflowed edges summarise whether a routing can be realised, and the congestion map tells placement and detailed routing where the trouble is.

## Overflowed edges

For an edge $e$ with demand $d_e$ and capacity $c_e$, the overflow is $o_e = \max(0, d_e - c_e)$. An edge is overflowed when $d_e > c_e$: more wires want to cross the boundary than there are tracks. Every overflowed edge is a place where detailed routing will have to detour, or fail.

Example: edges with (demand, capacity) of (5, 7), (5, 4), (16, 14) and (7, 8) have overflows 0, 1, 2 and 0, so two edges are overflowed and the worst overflows by 2. A congestion map colours each edge or gcell by utilisation $d_e / c_e$ or by overflow, which makes hot spots visible to a designer and machine-readable for a placer.

## Total and maximum overflow

Total overflow (TOF) sums the overflow over all edges, $\sum_e \max(0, d_e - c_e)$, and maximum overflow (MOF) is the largest single value. The ISPD 2007 and 2008 global-routing contests ranked routers first by total overflow and then by wirelength, so TOF became the standard figure of merit.

Example: overflows of 2, 2, 0, 0, 0 and 1 give TOF 5 and MOF 2. Under-used edges do not offset over-used ones, because each term is clipped at zero: slack on one edge does not help a net that must cross another. A routing with TOF 0 respects every estimated capacity; one with a small TOF spread thinly may still detail-route, while the same TOF concentrated in one region usually will not.

## Moving demand

Rip-up and reroute changes overflow by moving demand. Taking $k$ wires off edge $a$ and putting them on edge $b$ changes TOF by the change in $\max(0, d_a - c_a)$ plus the change in $\max(0, d_b - c_b)$. It helps only if $b$ has slack: moving 3 wires off an edge overflowed by 3 onto an edge already at capacity simply moves the overflow.

Example: $e_1$ at demand 14, capacity 11 and $e_7$ at 4, capacity 4. Moving 3 wires gives $e_1$ 11 of 11 and $e_7$ 7 of 4, and TOF is unchanged. Global routers therefore price edges by a cost that rises steeply near capacity, so the search naturally prefers edges with slack, and they accept small detours to buy reductions in overflow.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the ISPD 2007 and 2008 global routing contest descriptions.

label: Probabilistic congestion estimation
prereqs: Expectation of a function of a random variable
lesson:
# Probabilistic congestion estimation

Before routing, a placer or an early flow step needs to know where congestion will be. Probabilistic estimators guess each net's route distribution without searching: a two-pin connection is assumed to take each of its L shapes with equal probability, and demand on an edge is the expected number of nets crossing it. The estimate is cheap, smooth and good enough to steer placement.

## Expected demand of one net

Take a two-pin connection from $a$ to $b$ that differs in both coordinates. Its horizontal-first L runs along $a$'s row from $a$'s column to $b$'s, then vertically; its vertical-first L runs vertically first, then along $b$'s row. With each L chosen with probability 1/2, a horizontal edge in $a$'s row between the two columns gets expected demand 1/2 from this net, and so does one in $b$'s row. A net in a single row is straight and puts demand 1 on every edge it crosses.

Example: a net from (6, 1) to (1, 0) crosses the horizontal edge between (5, 0) and (6, 0) only on the L that runs along row 0, so its expected demand there is 0.5. Edges outside the pins' bounding box get nothing.

## Summing many nets

By linearity of expectation, the expected demand on an edge is the sum of the per-net expected demands, whatever the dependence between nets. Example: three nets contributing 0.5, 0 and 0.5 to an edge give expected demand 1. Doing this for every edge and net gives an expected-demand map in time proportional to the total bounding-box perimeter, with no search at all.

Variants spread demand over Z shapes too, or uniformly over all monotone routes, which smears demand into the interior of each bounding box. RUDY goes further and spreads each net's wire area uniformly over its box. All share the property that matters for a placer: they are cheap and change smoothly when a cell moves, so they can be evaluated inside an optimisation loop.

## Expected overflow is not overflow of the expectation

Capacity checks need overflow, not demand, and overflow is a convex function of demand: $o = \max(0, d - c)$. By Jensen's inequality, $E[\max(0, D - c)] \ge \max(0, E[D] - c)$, often strictly. Treating the nets' choices as independent, the exact expected overflow comes from enumerating (or convolving) the distribution of demand.

Example: four nets each cross an edge with probability 1/2, so $E[D] = 2$, and capacity is 2. Plugging the mean gives zero overflow, but $D$ is binomial: $P(D = 3) = 4/16$ and $P(D = 4) = 1/16$, so the expected overflow is $0.25 + 2/16 = 0.375$. An estimator that thresholds the mean map underestimates trouble exactly at edges near capacity, which are the ones that matter.

lesson:
# Global routing as an integer program

Global routing has an exact formulation as an integer linear program: pick one candidate tree per net so that no edge exceeds its capacity and total cost is minimal. Real instances are far too large to solve exactly, but the formulation is the reference that negotiation, Lagrangian methods and flow relaxations approximate, and it is how you reason about what an optimal router would do.

## Variables: one per candidate tree

For each net $i$, generate a set of candidate Steiner trees $T_{i1}, \dots, T_{ik_i}$ (for example, pattern routes of a FLUTE topology). Introduce a binary variable $x_{ij} = 1$ if net $i$ uses tree $j$. The program has $\sum_i k_i$ variables. Example: six nets with 3, 6, 6, 5, 2 and 5 candidates give 27 variables.

The candidate set is a modelling choice. With all possible trees the program is exact but has exponentially many variables; with a few candidates per net it is small but can only pick among them. Column generation adds candidate trees on demand, guided by dual prices from the LP relaxation, which is how exact-leaning routers keep the set small.

## Constraints and objective

Two families of constraints define a legal choice. Each net picks exactly one tree: $\sum_j x_{ij} = 1$ for every net $i$. Each edge respects capacity: $\sum_{i,j : e \in T_{ij}} x_{ij} \le c_e$ for every edge $e$. The objective minimises total cost, usually wirelength: $\min \sum_{i,j} w_{ij} x_{ij}$.

So there are as many selection constraints as nets and as many capacity constraints as edges. Example: 316 nets on a 20 by 12 gcell grid give $316 + 448 = 764$ constraints. A softer version replaces hard capacity with overflow variables penalised in the objective, which is always feasible and lets the solver report where capacity must be violated.

## Solving a tiny instance

For three nets with two candidates each, there are $2^3 = 8$ combinations. Check each against every capacity, discard the infeasible ones, and take the cheapest of the rest. That brute force is what branch and bound does cleverly: it relaxes $x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ to $0 \le x_{ij} \le 1$, solves the LP, and branches on fractional variables, pruning subtrees whose LP bound exceeds the best feasible cost.

The program is NP-hard in general, and full-chip instances have millions of variables, so production routers do not solve it. They use it as a reference: negotiated congestion behaves like Lagrangian relaxation of the capacity constraints, LP relaxation with randomised rounding gives provable bounds, and ILP on small windows is used for local refinement.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); P. Raghavan and C. D. Thompson, "Randomized Rounding: A Technique for Provably Good Algorithms and Algorithmic Proofs" (1987).

label: Global routing as multicommodity flow

lesson:
# Global routing as multicommodity flow

Viewed as network flow, global routing is a multicommodity flow problem: each two-pin connection is a commodity that must send one unit from its source to its sink, and all commodities share edge capacities. Without integrality it is a linear program solvable in polynomial time, and its relaxations give lower bounds and fractional solutions that rounding turns into routes.

## Flow variables

For commodity $k$ (a two-pin connection) and directed arc $(u, v)$, let $f^k_{uv} \ge 0$ be the flow of $k$ on that arc. Each undirected gcell edge gives two arcs, so on a grid with $E$ edges there are $2E$ arcs and $K \cdot 2E$ flow variables for $K$ commodities.

Example: a 5 by 12 gcell grid has $4 \cdot 12 + 5 \cdot 11 = 103$ edges and 206 arcs, so 35 commodities need 7210 variables. Integer flows correspond to routes: if all $f^k$ are 0 or 1 and conserve flow, they trace a path (possibly with cycles that can be removed). The size grows with nets times edges, which is why exact flow formulations are used on small regions or with heavy decomposition.

## Conservation and capacity

Flow conservation holds for every commodity at every vertex: outflow minus inflow equals 1 at the commodity's source, -1 at its sink and 0 elsewhere. That is $K \cdot V$ equations. Capacity couples the commodities: for each edge, the total flow of all commodities in both directions is at most $c_e$.

Example: 28 commodities on a 15 by 3 grid of 45 vertices give 1260 conservation equations. Without the capacity constraints the problem splits into $K$ independent shortest-path problems, one per commodity. All the difficulty, and all the interaction between nets, lives in the capacity rows, which is exactly what Lagrangian relaxation prices with multipliers and what negotiated congestion prices with present and history costs.

## Min-max utilisation

A common variant minimises the worst utilisation $\lambda$: total flow on each edge must be at most $\lambda c_e$. If the optimum has $\lambda \le 1$, a fractional routing fits every capacity; if $\lambda > 1$, no routing fits, even fractionally, so the instance is provably congested. This gives the router a certificate that integral heuristics cannot.

Example: edge flows of 5.5, 7, 12.5 and 4.5 over capacities 6, 4, 7 and 6 give utilisations 0.92, 1.75, 1.79 and 0.75, so $\lambda = 1.79$ for this solution. Approximation schemes for min-max multicommodity flow (in the style of Garg and Koenemann) update edge lengths multiplicatively with utilisation and reroute, which looks very much like negotiated congestion with an exponential present cost.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); N. Garg and J. Koenemann, "Faster and Simpler Algorithms for Multicommodity Flow and Other Fractional Packing Problems" (1998).

label: Negotiated-congestion global routing
lesson:
# Negotiated-congestion global routing

Negotiated congestion, introduced as PathFinder by McMurchie and Ebeling for FPGA routing, is the dominant global-routing strategy. Every net is routed by a shortest-path search on costs that rise with present overuse and with a history of past overuse. Nets that have alternatives move away from contested resources, and nets without alternatives keep them.

## The PathFinder cost

For a resource $n$ (a gcell edge, a track, an FPGA wire), PathFinder charges $c_n = (b_n + h_n)\,p_n$. Here $b_n$ is the base cost (length or delay), $h_n$ the history cost and $p_n$ the present-congestion factor, $p_n = 1 + p_{fac}\max(0, occ_n + 1 - cap_n)$, where $occ_n$ counts the nets already using $n$ and the $+1$ accounts for the net being routed.

Example: $b_n = 3$, $h_n = 0.5$, capacity 1, occupancy 3 and $p_{fac} = 2$ give $p_n = 1 + 2 \cdot 3 = 7$ and $c_n = 3.5 \cdot 7 = 24.5$. An edge with spare capacity has $p_n = 1$ and costs only $b_n + h_n$. The multiplicative form means history matters most on edges that are also presently congested.

## Routing on negotiated costs

Each iteration rips up and reroutes every net (or every net on an overflowed resource) with a shortest-path search, A* or Dijkstra, on the current costs. Occupancies update as nets are routed, so later nets in the same iteration see the congestion earlier nets created. A short path through full edges can then cost more than a longer path through free ones.

Example: path A has four edges at or above capacity and path B has five free edges with some history. With $p_{fac} = 0.5$, A might cost 5 and B 8.5, so the net still takes A. As $p_{fac}$ grows in later iterations, A's cost rises and the net moves, or another net sharing A's edges moves instead. The net that has the cheaper alternative is the one that yields: that is the negotiation.

## Raising the price over iterations

PathFinder starts with a small $p_{fac}$, so early iterations allow sharing and let each net find its preferred region, then multiplies $p_{fac}$ by a factor (often between 1.3 and 2) every iteration. Sharing becomes ever more expensive until no resource is overused. Example: $p_{fac} = 1$ in iteration 1 doubling each iteration gives 4 in iteration 3, so an edge at capacity 3 with occupancy 3, $b = 1$ and $h = 1.5$ costs $2.5 \cdot 5 = 12.5$.

The schedule is a speed-quality knob: grow too fast and nets freeze into the first legal-looking configuration with long detours; grow too slowly and runtime balloons. The method resembles Lagrangian relaxation of the capacity constraints, with the present and history terms acting as adaptive multipliers. It is also the template for global routers such as NCTU-GR and the negotiation loop in OpenROAD's grt.

## Going deeper

L. McMurchie and C. Ebeling, "PathFinder: A Negotiation-Based Performance-Driven Router for FPGAs" (1995); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the VPR routing documentation.

label: History costs in negotiated congestion
lesson:
# History costs in negotiated congestion

Present-congestion cost alone can make a router oscillate: two nets swap the same contested edge back and forth forever. History cost breaks the cycle. Each edge accumulates a penalty for every iteration it ends overused, and that memory makes chronically congested edges permanently expensive, so nets learn to avoid them even when they happen to fit for a moment.

## Accumulating history

After each iteration, every resource's history grows by its overuse: $h_n \leftarrow h_n + h_{fac}\max(0, occ_n - cap_n)$, starting from 0. History never decreases. Example: an edge of capacity 5 ends four iterations with occupancies 6, 4, 8 and 7; with $h_{fac} = 0.5$ it gains 0.5, 0, 1.5 and 1, so its history is 3.

Note the asymmetry with the present factor, which uses $occ_n + 1 - cap_n$ because it prices adding one more net now. History records what actually happened at the end of each iteration, so it uses $occ_n - cap_n$. An edge that was overused in iteration 2 stays more expensive in iteration 10 even if nobody overuses it in between.

## History moves stubborn nets

Consider a net whose short path A crosses one hot edge and whose alternative B is longer but free. Ignoring present cost, A costs $b_A + h$ and B costs $b_B$. If the hot edge ends every iteration overused by $o$, its history after $i - 1$ iterations is $(i-1) h_{fac} o$, and A first becomes more expensive in the smallest iteration $i$ with $b_A + (i-1) h_{fac} o > b_B$.

Example: $b_A = 9$, $b_B = 14$, $o = 1$ and $h_{fac} = 1$: A loses in iteration 7. Without history, if present cost alone left A slightly cheaper for this net every time it was rerouted, the net would never move and the edge would stay overused. History guarantees that persistent congestion eventually outweighs any finite path-length advantage.

## History and present cost together

In PathFinder the two terms combine as $(b_n + h_n)\,p_n$. History raises the floor of an edge's cost; the present factor multiplies it when the edge is full right now. Example: an edge with $b = 1$, capacity 4 and end-of-iteration occupancies 3 and 4 has history 0 (it was never overused). In iteration 3 with 5 nets already on it and $p_{fac} = 1$, its present factor is $1 + 2 = 3$ and its cost is 3.

The two factors must be tuned together. A large $h_{fac}$ converges quickly but can lock nets out of regions they need; a small one lets oscillation persist. Global routers such as NCTU-GR and NTHU-Route use history-based costs of this kind, often with variations such as letting history decay or scaling it by an edge's capacity.

## Going deeper

L. McMurchie and C. Ebeling, "PathFinder" (1995); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).
