label: Rip-up and reroute
lesson:
# Rip-up and reroute

Rip-up and reroute is the outer loop of every practical router: remove the nets that cause overflow and route them again on updated costs. Which nets to rip, in what order to reroute them, and how many iterations to run are policy choices that strongly affect quality and runtime, and they are the natural place to customise a router.

## Which nets to rip up

After an initial routing, compute demand on every edge and find the overflowed edges. The standard choice rips up every net that uses at least one overflowed edge; a gentler one rips up only enough of them to clear each edge, preferring nets with cheap alternatives. Nets on uncongested edges are left in place, which keeps each iteration fast and preserves good routes.

Example: with eight edges and five nets, if edges $e_4$ and $e_8$ are overflowed, every net whose route includes $e_4$ or $e_8$ is ripped up, here perhaps three of the five. Ripping more nets explores more but wastes effort on nets that were fine; ripping fewer converges slowly.

## Reroute ordering

The ripped nets are rerouted one at a time, so their order matters: earlier nets see less congestion. Common rules sort by bounding-box size. Smallest first lets short nets with few alternatives claim the resources they need before long nets, which can detour, take them. Largest first settles the long nets that block many others while space remains. Other rules use the amount of overflow a net touches, its criticality or its pin count.

Example: ripped nets with half-perimeters 27, 15 and 13 rerouted largest first go in the order 27, 15, 13. Negotiation reduces the sensitivity to order, because prices adjust across iterations, but order still affects runtime and the final wirelength.

## Measuring a reroute

Each reroute removes the net's demand from its old edges and adds it to the new ones. The effect on total overflow is the sum of changes on every edge touched. Example: a net moved from $e_1, e_3$ onto $e_4, e_5, e_8$ may relieve $e_1$ but push $e_4$ and $e_8$ over capacity, raising total overflow from 1 to 2. A good reroute uses edge costs that rise steeply near capacity, so the search avoids exactly that.

Loops stop when overflow reaches zero, stops improving, or an iteration budget runs out. Production global routers combine rip-up and reroute with negotiation (history and present costs), escalating from pattern routing to monotonic to bounded maze routing for the hardest nets, and they report the residual overflow map when they cannot clear it.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); the NTHU-Route 2.0 and NCTU-GR 2.0 papers.

label: FastRoute, NCTU-GR and OpenROAD grt
lesson:
# FastRoute, NCTU-GR and OpenROAD grt

The research ideas of global routing, FLUTE trees, pattern and monotonic routing, negotiated congestion with history and bounded maze search, are combined in open global routers such as FastRoute and NCTU-GR, and in OpenROAD's grt. Knowing how they are composed, and what they hand to detailed routing, is what you need to read or modify these tools.

## The FastRoute pipeline

FastRoute (Pan and Chu, with later versions by Xu, Zhang and Chu) builds each net's topology with FLUTE, reshapes the tree for congestion, decomposes it into two-pin connections and routes them by L and Z patterns. Later versions added monotonic routing and multi-source multi-sink maze routing, virtual capacities that steer negotiation, and via-aware routing with layer assignment. Maze routing is applied only to connections that patterns leave overflowed.

OpenROAD's global router, grt, is based on FastRoute. It reads LEF and DEF, builds the gcell grid with layer adjustments, routes, and writes route guides: rectangles per net and layer that the detailed router, drt, must stay inside. It also reports the congestion map that placement and the designer use.

## Negotiation in practice

Contest-era routers such as NTHU-Route 2.0 and NCTU-GR built on negotiation: every iteration reroutes the nets on overflowed edges with a cost that combines present congestion and history, and searches are bounded to a box around the net so they stay fast and avoid long detours. NCTU-GR 2.0 also routed nets in parallel, scheduling together nets whose regions do not overlap so their demand updates cannot collide.

The ISPD 2007 and 2008 benchmarks scored total overflow first, then wirelength, which shaped these designs: they spend most of their time clearing the last few overflowed edges. A useful mental model is pattern routing for the many easy nets, negotiation with maze search for the few hard ones.

## Using a global router in a flow

Many global routers route in 2D, on the projection with capacities summed over layers, and assign layers afterwards, because negotiation converges much faster on the smaller graph. Layer assignment then has to fit each 2D route into the per-layer capacities while minimising vias, which can reintroduce overflow on individual layers.

A global router is also a fast analysis engine. Routability-driven placement calls it, or a cheaper estimate, to find hot spots; a truncated run with fewer iterations and pattern routing only produces a usable congestion map early in a flow. If the final result has a little overflow concentrated in a few gcells, the right move is usually local: spread placement there or adjust capacity, rather than hoping detailed routing absorbs it.

## Going deeper

M. Pan and C. Chu, "FastRoute" (2006) and "FastRoute 2.0" (2007); Y. Xu, Y. Zhang and C. Chu, "FastRoute 4.0: Global Router with Efficient Via Minimization" (2009); the OpenROAD grt documentation.

label: Layer assignment and via minimization
lesson:
# Layer assignment and via minimization

Many global routers route on a 2D projection and only afterwards assign each wire segment to a metal layer. Layer assignment decides via count, and vias matter: each adds resistance, blocks tracks on the layers it passes through and is a yield risk. Counting the vias of an assignment, and knowing when it is minimal, is the starting point for every assignment algorithm.

## Counting vias of a path

In a preferred-direction stack each segment of a route sits on a layer of its own direction. A via stack between layers $a$ and $b$ counts $|a - b|$ vias. For a two-pin route with pins on metal 1 and segments on layers $l_1, \dots, l_n$, the via count is
$$(l_1 - 1) + \sum_{i=2}^{n} |l_i - l_{i-1}| + (l_n - 1).$$

Example: with M2, M4 and M6 horizontal and M3, M5 and M7 vertical, a route H on M4, V on M5, H on M4, V on M7 needs $3 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 6 = 14$ vias: 3 down to the first pin, one at each of the first two bends, 3 at the last bend and 6 down to the second pin. Long via stacks to pins are why upper layers are expensive for short nets.

## The minimum for a fixed 2D route

For a two-pin route whose directions alternate, putting every horizontal segment on the lowest horizontal layer and every vertical segment on the lowest vertical layer minimises vias. Every bend needs at least one via (adjacent segments are on different layers), and each pin needs at least the stack to the lowest layer of its segment's direction, and the lowest assignment achieves exactly those bounds.

Example: an assignment using 12 vias for a five-segment route drops to $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$ on M2 and M3 (one via up from the first pin to M2, four bends, one down from M2 at the end), saving 6. Real assigners do not do this, because the lowest layers would overflow. The minimum is the baseline, and the question becomes how many vias to spend to fit capacity and meet timing.

## Vias at junctions

In a multipin tree, several segments meet at a Steiner point or a pin. The via stack at such a point must reach every layer used there, so it spans from the lowest to the highest: $\max(S) - \min(S)$ vias for the set $S$ of layers meeting at the point (including metal 1 if a pin is there). Two collinear segments on the same layer meeting at a junction need no via between them.

Example: a junction where horizontal segments on M6 and M6 meet a vertical branch on M5 needs one via. A tree's total via count sums these stacks over all junctions, bends and pins. This is why layer assignment works on whole trees, usually by dynamic programming from the leaves up: a choice on one branch changes the stack at the junction it shares with others.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); Y. Xu, Y. Zhang and C. Chu, "FastRoute 4.0" (2009) on via-aware layer assignment.

label: Layer assignment by dynamic programming
lesson:
# Layer assignment by dynamic programming

Layer assignment must respect per-layer capacity: after 2D routing, some layers are already full in some gcells. Choosing a layer for each segment so that vias are minimal and no full layer is used is a shortest-path problem on a small layered graph, solved exactly by dynamic programming along each route or tree.

## The recurrence

Number a two-pin route's segments $S_1, \dots, S_n$ from pin to pin, and let $A_i$ be the layers still free for $S_i$ (the right direction, with capacity left in the gcells it crosses). Define $D(i, l)$ as the fewest vias for $S_1$ to $S_i$ with $S_i$ on layer $l$, counting the first pin's stack. Then $D(1, l) = l - 1$ and
$$D(i, l) = \min_{p \in A_{i-1}} D(i-1, p) + |l - p|.$$
The answer closes with the second pin: $\min_{l \in A_n} D(n, l) + l - 1$.

Example: if $S_2$ can only use M5 or M7, the stack from a horizontal $S_1$ to $S_2$ is forced to climb, and the recurrence finds where the climb is cheapest.

## Reading one table entry

The table has one entry per segment and free layer, so a five-segment route with three choices each has at most 15 entries, each computed from at most three predecessors. That is linear in route length, which is why assigners can afford to run it on every net and rerun it after capacity changes.

Example: if $S_1$ is free on M2 and M6 and $S_2$ on M5 and M7, then $D(1, 2) = 1$, $D(1, 6) = 5$, and $D(2, 5) = \min(1 + 3, 5 + 1) = 4$. Remembering which predecessor won at each entry recovers the assignment by walking back from the best final entry. On trees, the same recurrence runs from the leaves to the root, with a junction's cost depending on the layers of all its children.

## Ties and real objectives

Many assignments often achieve the minimum via count. Counting them is a small extension: carry, alongside each entry, the number of predecessors achieving it, and add counts on ties. Example: a route with free layers on its middle segments might have 3 distinct assignments at the minimum of 12 vias.

Ties are an opportunity. A production assigner breaks them, or trades a via or two, for other goals: balancing demand across layers so no layer is near capacity, putting timing-critical nets on low-resistance upper layers, and keeping via density per gcell low. These become extra terms in the same recurrence, or a sequential order in which critical nets are assigned first and claim their layers.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); T.-H. Lee and T.-C. Wang, "Congestion-Constrained Layer Assignment for Via Minimization in Global Routing" (2008).

label: Timing-aware layer assignment
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Timing-aware layer assignment

Upper metal layers are thicker and wider, so their resistance per micron is far lower. Putting a long, timing-critical net on them cuts its delay, but reaching them costs a via stack at each end, which adds resistance and uses scarce capacity. Timing-aware layer assignment decides which nets earn the upper layers.

## Delay on a low layer

Model the net as a driver of resistance $R_d$ driving a distributed wire of length $L$ with resistance $r$ and capacitance $c$ per micron into a load $C_L$. Its Elmore delay is
$$T = R_d(cL + C_L) + rL\left(\frac{cL}{2} + C_L\right).$$
The first term charges everything through the driver; the second is the wire's own distributed RC, which grows with $L^2$.

Example: $R_d = 550$ ohm, $c = 0.25$ fF/um, $C_L = 10$ fF, $r = 2$ ohm/um and $L = 200$ um give $550 \cdot 60 + 400 \cdot 35 = 47000$ ohm-fF, which is 47 ps. One ohm times one femtofarad is one femtosecond.

## Delay on an upper layer

Moving the wire to an upper layer replaces $r$ with a much smaller $r'$ but adds a via stack of $k$ vias of resistance $R_v$ at each end. With the start stack in series with the driver and the end stack in front of the load,
$$T' = (R_d + kR_v)(cL + C_L) + r'L\left(\frac{cL}{2} + C_L\right) + kR_v C_L.$$
Capacitance per micron is similar on both layers in this simple model.

Example: $R_d = 850$ ohm, two 30-ohm vias at each end, $c = 0.25$ fF/um, $C_L = 6$ fF, $L = 950$ um, $r' = 0.2$ ohm/um against $r = 3$ ohm/um. The upper layer gives about 246 ps against about 563 ps on the low layer: for long wires the $L^2$ term dominates and the upper layer wins by a wide margin.

## Break-even length

The upper layer saves $(r - r')L(cL/2 + C_L)$ and pays $kR_v(cL + 2C_L)$. The saving grows like $L^2$ and the penalty like $L$, so there is a single break-even length: shorter nets are faster on low layers, longer ones on high layers. Scanning lengths (or solving the quadratic) finds it; for typical numbers it is a few hundred microns.

Upper-layer capacity is scarce, so assigners rank nets by how much slack they need and how much an upper layer would buy, and give the top layers to the nets with the biggest gain per track. Short nets with small timing benefit and large via cost are pushed down. The same reasoning drives non-default rules: wider wires on critical nets lower $r$ at the price of tracks.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.); S. Hu, Z. Li and C. J. Alpert, "A Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme for Timing Constrained Minimum Cost Layer Assignment" (2008).

label: Redundant via insertion
lesson:
# Redundant via insertion

A via is a small hole filled with metal, and a fraction of them fail open in manufacturing. A chip has billions of vias, so even a tiny failure probability adds up. Redundant via insertion places a second cut next to the first wherever space allows, so the connection fails only if both cuts fail. It is a standard post-routing step for yield.

## Expected via failures

If each of $N$ vias fails independently with probability $p$, the expected number of failures is $Np$ by linearity of expectation. Example: 15 million single-cut vias with $p = 5 \times 10^{-7}$ give 7.5 expected failures per die. Any one failure can kill the die if it opens a net, so this number is a direct yield risk.

Failure probabilities for single vias depend on the process, the via size and the surrounding layout; the independence assumption is a first-order model. Even so, it shows the scale: with $N$ in the billions, $p$ has to be extraordinarily small, or the vias must be made redundant.

## Doubling vias

A doubled via opens only if both of its cuts fail, with probability about $p^2$, which is negligible. If a fraction $r$ of $N$ via locations is doubled, the expected number of opens is $N[(1 - r)p + r p^2] \approx N(1 - r)p$. Example: 40 million vias at $p = 10^{-7}$ give 4 expected opens; doubling 52% of them leaves about 1.92.

So the benefit is set almost entirely by the doubling rate, and the remaining single vias dominate. That is why redundant via insertion tries to maximise the doubled fraction. Each candidate second cut needs room on both metal layers, so the problem is a maximum independent set or matching over conflicting candidates, solved heuristically or with integer programming on small windows.

## Via-limited yield

The probability that no via opens is $Y = (1 - p)^{N_s}(1 - p^2)^{N_d}$ for $N_s$ single and $N_d$ doubled vias, which is close to $e^{-N_s p}$. Example: 21 million vias at $p = 2 \times 10^{-7}$: with no doubling $Y = e^{-4.2} \approx 1.5\%$; doubling 63% leaves 7.77 million single vias and $Y \approx e^{-1.55} \approx 21\%$.

The router helps before insertion even runs. Via-aware detailed routing leaves space next to vias for a second cut, prefers via positions where a double fits, and avoids long via stacks. The cost is a little extra metal and some routing flexibility, which is why the doubling rate is a quality metric reported next to wirelength and DRC count.

## Going deeper

label: Track assignment
lesson:
# Track assignment

Between global and detailed routing, many flows run track assignment: the long horizontal or vertical runs that global routing put in a row or column of gcells (a panel) are assigned to specific tracks before any maze search. TritonRoute does this, and the problem is interval packing, the same mathematics as channel routing, with overlap as the cost of a bad assignment.

## Interval packing in a panel

In a horizontal panel each global segment covers an interval of gcells $[l, r]$. Two segments conflict if their intervals share a gcell: they cannot share a track there. The conflict graph is an interval graph, and interval graphs are perfect: the fewest tracks that hold all segments without conflict equals the largest clique, which is the maximum number of segments covering any one gcell.

Example: segments [17, 18], [12, 19], [18, 19], [1, 6] and [9, 14] all cover gcell 18 three at a time ([17, 18], [12, 19], [18, 19]), so the panel needs 3 tracks. A left-edge sweep, sorting segments by left end and placing each on the first track whose last segment ended before it, achieves the bound.

## Conflicts between segments

The conflict graph has an edge for every pair of segments that share a gcell. With $n$ segments there are $n(n-1)/2$ pairs to check, or a sort by left end finds the overlaps in $O(n \log n + k)$ for $k$ conflicts. Example: segments [16, 20], [4, 14], [5, 6], [13, 19] and [18, 20] have five conflicting pairs.

The edges are what a track assigner must keep apart, and they carry more than a yes or no: the overlap length matters, and so do soft conflicts, such as two segments on adjacent tracks running alongside an aggressor net, or a segment ending near a pin that its neighbour must reach. Real track assigners weigh all of these in one cost.

## Overlap cost when tracks run out

A panel often has fewer tracks than its density, so some overlap is unavoidable. A track assigner then minimises a cost such as total overlap: for every pair of segments on the same track, the number of gcells they share. Example: with three tracks, an assignment that puts [11, 18] and [14, 20] on one track pays 5, the length of [14, 18].

Every unit of overlap is work handed to detailed routing, which must resolve it by moving one segment off its track with a detour. Assigners therefore also consider pin positions, blockages and previously assigned nets, and solve greedily, with matching, or with iterative improvement. A good assignment lets the detailed router spend its time on pin access and rule details rather than on long rearrangements.

## Going deeper

A. B. Kahng, L. Wang and B. Xu, "TritonRoute: The Open-Source Detailed Router" (IEEE TCAD, 2021); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Pin access points
lesson:
# Pin access points

Standard-cell pins at advanced nodes are small, crowded shapes on the lowest layers, and reaching them legally is one of the hardest parts of detailed routing. Pin-access analysis enumerates, for each pin, the points where a via or wire can land without violating rules, and chooses combinations that do not block each other. A router that gets this wrong fails locally no matter how good its global plan is.

## On-track access points

An access point is a location on a pin where a via up to the next routing layer can land. With vertical M2 tracks at $x = o + kp$, a via on track $x$ fits inside a pin spanning $[x_1, x_2]$ only if its metal landing fits with the required enclosure $e$ on each side: $x_1 + e \le x \le x_2 - e$.

Example: tracks at $40 + 80k$ nm, $e = 10$ nm and a pin from 320 to 630 nm give the window [330, 620], which holds tracks 360, 440, 520 and 600: four access points. A pin narrower than one pitch plus twice the enclosure may have none at all on track, which is a real failure mode in dense libraries.

## Compatible choices for neighbours

Access points of neighbouring pins interact. Two vias too close together violate via-to-via spacing, and a via on one pin can block the only access of the next. So pin-access engines choose a combination of access points per cell instance: one point for each pin such that every pair is legal.

Example: pin A with an access point at 196 nm and pin B with points at 308 and 364 nm, with vias required at least 112 nm apart. Both pairs (196, 308) and (196, 364) qualify, so 2 combinations remain. Since cells repeat, engines analyse each unique cell and placement context once and reuse the result across all its instances, which is what makes the enumeration affordable.

## Off-track access

When on-track points are too few, an engine also considers off-track positions, for example halfway between tracks. A via there is joined to a nearby track by a short jog, which must itself be DRC-clean. Example: allowing half-track positions in a pin window [305, 425] with tracks every 56 nm turns 3 on-track points into 5 candidates.

Off-track access trades simplicity for success. It raises the number of choices, which helps crowded cells, but every jog is extra metal near other pins, so the engine must check spacing, end-of-line and minimum-area rules on it. TritonRoute's pin-access step generates on-track and off-track candidates in this spirit, validates each against the rules, and prefers clean, on-track ones.

## Going deeper

A. B. Kahng, L. Wang and B. Xu, "The Tao of PAO: Anatomy of a Pin Access Oracle for Detailed Routing" (DAC 2020); the TritonRoute paper (IEEE TCAD, 2021).

label: DRC-aware detailed routing
prereqs: Bend and via costs in maze routing
lesson:
# DRC-aware detailed routing

A detailed router's output must satisfy every rule in the deck: spacing, width, end-of-line, minimum area, via enclosure and more. DRC-aware routing builds those rules into the search, as costs on candidate moves and as blocked resources, so that the router produces clean wires rather than finding violations afterwards. This is the core of what makes a detailed router hard to write.

## Pricing violations

During search a detailed router lets a route pass through states that would create a violation, but charges for it: a route's cost is its length plus a cost per via plus a large penalty per design-rule violation it would create. Example: 18 steps, 5 vias at 5 each and one violation at 100 cost $18 + 25 + 100 = 143$.

Why not forbid violations outright? Because early in routing a short route with a violation may be the only way through, and the violation can be fixed later by moving a different net. Soft penalties keep the search complete while steering it toward legality, and the penalty grows during repair so that the final result is clean.

## Choosing among candidates

Given candidates for one connection, the router keeps the cheapest under its costs. Example: route A has 50 steps, 3 vias and no violation; B has 31 steps, 4 vias and 2 violations; C has 32 steps, 2 vias and none. With via cost 6 and violation cost 50, the costs are 68, 155 and 44, so C wins: clean and short.

The relative weights encode policy. A violation penalty much larger than any plausible detour makes the router prefer clean routes almost always. A penalty too small lets it leave violations everywhere, and one too large freezes nets that should move. Production routers tune these weights per stage and grow them across repair iterations.

## Rules as blocked tracks

Some rules are cheaper to model as blocked resources than to check per move. A wide wire needs more spacing to its neighbours than a normal wire; a spacing table gives the required value by width. With track pitch $p$, normal width $w$ and a wide wire of width $W$, the edge gap to a wire on the $k$-th track over is $kp - W/2 - w/2$. Every track where that gap is below the wide-wire spacing is blocked.

Example: $p = 48$ nm, $w = 24$ nm, $W = 96$ nm and a required spacing of 94 nm. The gaps to tracks 1 to 4 are -12, 36, 84 and 132 nm (a negative gap means the wires would overlap), so tracks 1 to 3 on each side are blocked and track 4 is the first usable one. Precomputing such blockages turns rule checking into graph editing, which keeps the search kernel fast.

## Going deeper

The TritonRoute paper (IEEE TCAD, 2021); the OpenROAD drt documentation; the LEF reference for SPACINGTABLE and related rules.

lesson:
# Minimum-area and end-of-line rules

Beyond spacing, modern rule decks constrain the shape of every wire end. Minimum-area rules forbid tiny isolated metal, end-of-line rules require extra room in front of a line end, and via enclosure rules require metal around each cut. A detailed router has to generate shapes that satisfy all of them at once, which is why short stubs and line ends are where violations cluster.

## Minimum area

Lithography cannot reliably print very small isolated shapes, so each layer has a minimum area $A_{min}$. A stub of width $w$ needs length at least $A_{min}/w$, rounded up to the manufacturing grid. Example: $A_{min} = 9000$ nm$^2$ and $w = 28$ nm need $9000/28 = 321.4$, so 322 nm; a 209 nm stub must grow by 113 nm.

The router fixes this by extending the wire end in its direction, which may itself collide with neighbours, so the extension is part of the search or of a post-processing patch with its own checks. Via landing pads on a layer that carries nothing else are the classic case: the pad is tiny unless deliberately grown.

## End-of-line spacing

Two line ends facing each other on the same track need a larger gap than the normal side-to-side spacing, because line ends print shorter and rounder than drawn. The end-of-line rule requires facing ends to be at least $s_{eol}$ apart. Checking a track is a sweep: sort its segments, subtract each end from the next start, and flag every gap below $s_{eol}$.

Example: segments [0, 83], [153, 256], [296, 566] with $s_{eol} = 50$ nm have gaps 70 and 40, so one violation. Routers price line ends that stop too close to another, and prefer to extend a wire through a short gap (merging the ends) or to shift where it ends. Full end-of-line rules also look sideways within a window, which makes them context dependent and expensive to evaluate.

## Rules that interact

A via lands on a metal stub that must enclose the cut by $e$ beyond each end in the wire direction, so the stub needs length at least $v + 2e$ for cut length $v$. The same stub must also meet minimum area. So the required length is $\max(v + 2e, \lceil A_{min}/w \rceil)$.

Example: a 32 nm cut with 30 nm enclosure needs 92 nm, while $A_{min} = 7000$ nm$^2$ at width 32 nm needs 219 nm, so the stub must be 219 nm. Rules like these stack, and some are conditional on neighbours (end-of-line within a parallel run, spacing by width and run length). That is why routers evaluate shapes against the full rule deck with a geometric engine rather than one formula, and why rule changes between PDK versions break hard-coded router logic.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF reference on MINAREA, SPACING ENDOFLINE and via rules; the TritonRoute paper (IEEE TCAD, 2021).

problems.e: The stub needs length at least 19000 / 32 = 593.75 nm, so 594 nm after rounding up, an extension of 429 nm.

label: Search-and-repair DRC loops
lesson:
# Search-and-repair DRC loops

No detailed router produces a clean layout in one pass. After initial routing, a search-and-repair loop finds the remaining violations, rips up the nets around them, raises the cost of the offending locations and reroutes, over and over, until the violation count reaches zero or stops falling. The schedule of this loop decides runtime and final quality.

## Marker penalties

After a pass, the design-rule checker leaves markers at every violation. The router adds a penalty to grid cells covered by markers, so that rerouted nets avoid them. To make the loop converge, the penalty grows across iterations: in iteration $i$ a marked cell might cost $b + m_0 g^{i-1}$ for base cost $b$, initial penalty $m_0$ and growth factor $g$.

Example: $b = 3$, $m_0 = 8$ and $g = 2$ give a marked cell a cost of $3 + 128 = 131$ in iteration 5. Early iterations tolerate violations so nets can find their way; later ones make violations so expensive that any clean detour wins. This mirrors negotiated congestion, applied to rule violations instead of capacity.

## When the detour wins

A net crossing $n_m$ marked cells keeps its short route until the marker penalty outweighs the extra length of a clean detour $d$. With a penalty $m_0 2^{i-1}$, the detour first wins in the smallest iteration $i$ with $n_m m_0 2^{i-1} > d$. Example: one marked cell, $m_0 = 1$, a detour 35 cells longer: the penalty first exceeds 35 at 64, in iteration 7.

This calculation explains loop behaviour. A violation with a cheap detour clears in a couple of iterations; one whose only fix is a long detour or the cooperation of several nets lingers. A geometric schedule bounds the wait logarithmically in the detour length, which is why repair loops typically run a few tens of iterations rather than hundreds.

## Clip-based repair

Repair works locally. The router cuts the region into clips of a few gcells, and in each iteration reroutes only the clips that contain markers, keeping wires crossing the clip boundary fixed so the clip behaves like a switchbox. Clip boundaries shift between iterations, so a violation that sat on a boundary lands inside a clip next time.

Example: with 5 by 5 clips offset by one gcell, a marker at gcell (6, 34) falls in clip (1, 7). Mapping every marker and counting distinct clips gives the work for the iteration. Local repair keeps each pass cheap and parallel, since clips can be routed independently, and it limits collateral damage to nets that were already clean. TritonRoute and OpenROAD's drt run search-and-repair in this clip-based style.

## Going deeper

The TritonRoute paper (IEEE TCAD, 2021); the OpenROAD drt documentation on detailed-routing iterations.

problems.q: A search-and-repair detailed router marks every grid cell touched by a DRC violation. Each cell costs 2 to cross, plus a marker penalty on marked cells that is 2 in repair iteration 1 and is multiplied by 2 at each further iteration. How much does crossing one marked cell cost in iteration 4?
problems.e: The penalty in iteration 4 is 2 x 2^3 = 16, so the cell costs 2 + 16 = 18. Growing penalties push the nets causing the violation away from it a little more each pass.

problems.q: A search-and-repair detailed router marks every grid cell touched by a DRC violation. Each cell costs 3 to cross, plus a marker penalty on marked cells that is 5 in repair iteration 1 and is multiplied by 3 at each further iteration. How much does crossing one marked cell cost in iteration 1?
problems.e: The penalty in iteration 1 is 5 x 3^0 = 5, so the cell costs 3 + 5 = 8. Growing penalties push the nets causing the violation away from it a little more each pass.

problems.q: A search-and-repair detailed router marks every grid cell touched by a DRC violation. Each cell costs 1 to cross, plus a marker penalty on marked cells that is 2 in repair iteration 1 and is multiplied by 2 at each further iteration. How much does crossing one marked cell cost in iteration 5?
problems.e: The penalty in iteration 5 is 2 x 2^4 = 32, so the cell costs 1 + 32 = 33. Growing penalties push the nets causing the violation away from it a little more each pass.

The marker penalty per marked cell is 1 in iteration 1 and doubles at each further iteration; unmarked cells cost the same on both routes. In which iteration does the detour first become strictly cheaper?
problems.e: The detour wins when 1 x penalty > 20. The penalty is 1 x 2^(i - 1), which first exceeds 20 / 1 in iteration 6 (penalty 32). Until then the router keeps the short, dirty route.

label: Coloring-aware detailed routing
lesson:
# Coloring-aware detailed routing

At advanced nodes the tightest metal layers are printed with multiple masks: features too close for one exposure are split between masks. That turns every routing decision into a coloring problem, because two nearby wires must land on different masks. A coloring-aware detailed router avoids creating conflicts that no mask assignment can satisfy, rather than leaving them for decomposition to fail on.

## The conflict graph

Build a graph with one vertex per wire shape on the layer and an edge between any two shapes closer than the same-mask spacing. A legal mask assignment is a proper coloring with as many colors as masks: two masks for litho-etch-litho-etch double patterning (LELE), three for triple patterning.

The layout is decomposable with two masks exactly when the conflict graph is bipartite, that is, has no odd cycle. Example: wires on adjacent tracks conflict where they run alongside each other; those conflicts alone are always two-colorable by track parity. But if two wires on the same track also end too close tip to tip, they conflict too, and a tip-to-tip edge on one track with paths through the neighbouring track can close an odd cycle, which forces a third mask.

## Counting conflicts from geometry

Conflicts come from geometry: adjacent tracks with overlapping x ranges, or the same track with a tip-to-tip gap below the same-mask limit. Example: wires [5, 63] and [103, 194] on track 1, [15, 89] and [99, 159] on track 2, with a tip-to-tip limit of 30 nm: the track-2 wires are 10 nm apart and conflict, the track-1 wires are 40 nm apart and do not, and each pair of overlapping wires across tracks 1 and 2 conflicts.

The edge count measures how constrained the layer is. A router that knows the coloring rules prices moves that add edges, especially edges that would close an odd cycle, and prefers line-end positions that keep tip-to-tip gaps above the limit.

## Coloring violations

Given a proposed mask assignment, a coloring violation is a conflict edge whose two shapes share a mask. Example: if a decomposer colors wires by track parity but two same-track wires conflict tip to tip, every such pair is a violation, because they necessarily share a color.

Violations are fixed by rerouting one of the shapes (moving a line end, changing track), or where the process allows, by a stitch that splits one shape across both masks at the cost of overlay risk. Coloring-aware routers either carry a color with each wire during search (correct by construction) or route first and repair coloring conflicts like any other violation. In self-aligned double patterning (SADP) the rules are different again, since line ends and cuts, not adjacency alone, define what prints.

## Going deeper

D. Z. Pan, B. Yu and J.-R. Gao, "Design for Manufacturing with Emerging Nanolithography" (IEEE TCAD, 2013); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Channel density
lesson:
# Channel density

Channel routing is the classical detailed-routing problem: a rectangular region with pins on its top and bottom edges, nets that enter at those pins, horizontal trunks on tracks and vertical branches down to the pins. Its central lower bound is density, the most nets that must cross one column. The same interval reasoning reappears in track assignment and panel routing inside modern routers.

## Local density

Columns are numbered left to right; each column may hold a top pin and a bottom pin, each labelled with a net or empty. A net's trunk must span from its leftmost to its rightmost pin column. The local density at column $c$ is the number of nets whose span includes $c$; those nets all need a horizontal track at that column, and two of them cannot share one.

Example: with top pins 0, 4, 0, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1 and bottom pins 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 0, 4, the spans are net 1 [1, 8], net 2 [2, 7], net 3 [3, 6] and net 4 [2, 8], so column 7 has local density 3 (nets 1, 2 and 4).

## Channel density as a lower bound

The channel density $d$ is the maximum local density over all columns. Any routing that gives each net a single horizontal trunk needs at least $d$ tracks, because at the densest column $d$ trunks run in parallel. Computing it is a plane sweep: sort span endpoints, add one at each left end, subtract one after each right end, and track the maximum.

Example: spans [6, 7], [2, 6], [1, 5], [1, 4] and [7, 8] reach density 3 at columns 2 to 4. Density counts horizontal demand only. Vertical constraints between nets can force more tracks than density, which is why the left-edge algorithm achieves density only when there are no vertical constraints.

## Bottleneck columns

Several columns may attain the density. Each is a bottleneck: no rearrangement of trunks reduces the tracks needed there, so a channel router cannot use fewer than $d$ tracks, and every column at density pins down a set of nets that must be stacked. Example: spans [3, 7], [4, 5], [6, 8], [1, 8] and [1, 2] reach density 3 at four columns.

Channel heights in building-block layouts were set by these numbers, and reducing density meant changing the placement of pins. In modern flows the same quantity appears as gcell-edge demand in global routing and as panel density in track assignment. A router designer should read density as the horizontal capacity a region must supply, before any vertical interaction is considered.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), on channel routing; Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation", chapter on channel routing.

Each net's horizontal trunk spans from its leftmost to its rightmost pin column, inclusive. What is the local density at column 9, the number of nets whose span includes that column?

label: Horizontal and vertical constraint graphs
lesson:
# Horizontal and vertical constraint graphs

Channel routing has two kinds of constraint. Horizontal constraints say two trunks that overlap cannot share a track. Vertical constraints say that at a column with net a on top and net b at the bottom, a's trunk must lie above b's, or their vertical branches would cross on the same layer. The horizontal and vertical constraint graphs encode both, and together they bound and drive every channel router.

## The vertical constraint graph

In a two-layer channel with trunks on one layer and branches on the other, column $c$ with net $a$ at the top and a different net $b$ at the bottom has two vertical branches in the same column. To avoid overlapping, $a$'s trunk must be above $b$'s. The vertical constraint graph (VCG) has a directed edge $a \to b$ for every such column; repeated pairs give one edge.

Example: top pins 2, 3, 3, 0, 4 and bottom pins 0, 1, 4, 2, 1 give edges $3 \to 1$, $3 \to 4$ and $4 \to 1$: three distinct edges (columns with only one pin or with the same net on both sides give none).

## Longest chain as a lower bound

Each VCG edge forces the source net strictly above the target, so a directed path through $k$ nets forces $k$ distinct tracks. If the VCG is acyclic, the number of vertices on its longest path is a lower bound on tracks for any dogleg-free routing, computed by longest-path dynamic programming in topological order.

Example: a chain $3 \to 2 \to 5$ forces 3 tracks, even if the channel density is only 2. The tracks needed are at least $\max(d, \ell)$ for density $d$ and longest chain $\ell$. Neither bound is tight in general, because the two constraint types interact: a net forced low by the VCG may collide horizontally with nets that are also forced low.

## The horizontal constraint graph

The horizontal constraint graph (HCG) is undirected, with an edge between two nets whose spans share a column, so they cannot share a track. It is an interval graph: its largest clique is exactly the channel density, and without vertical constraints it can be colored with that many colors (tracks) by the left-edge algorithm.

Example: spans [4, 9], [3, 8], [4, 8], [2, 3] and [6, 9] give 7 overlapping pairs, and the largest clique is 4 (column 6 to 8). A channel router assigns tracks so that HCG neighbours differ and VCG edges point downward, which is a coloring of the HCG constrained by an order from the VCG.

## Going deeper

A. Hashimoto and J. Stevens, "Wire Routing by Optimizing Channel Assignment within Large Apertures" (1971); Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation".

label: Channel routing by the left-edge algorithm
lesson:
# Channel routing by the left-edge algorithm

The left-edge algorithm of Hashimoto and Stevens (1971) is the first and simplest channel router: sort trunks by left end and pack them greedily onto tracks. Without vertical constraints it is optimal; with them, a constrained version respects the vertical constraint graph by filling tracks from the top. It is still the template for interval packing in detailed routers.

## Unconstrained left edge

Sort the nets by the left end of their spans. Fill track 1: scan the sorted list and place each net whose left end lies to the right of the last net placed on the track. When the scan ends, start track 2 with the remaining nets, and so on.

Example: spans [9, 16], [4, 7], [3, 10], [2, 3] and [7, 10]. Track 1 takes [2, 3], then [4, 7], then [9, 16]; track 2 takes [3, 10]; track 3 takes [7, 10]. Three tracks, which equals the density: without vertical constraints the greedy is optimal, because when it opens a new track every existing track is busy at the current net's left end, so that many spans overlap there.

## Constrained left edge

With vertical constraints, fill tracks from the top. For each track, scan the unplaced nets by left end and add a net only if every net that must lie above it (its VCG predecessors) is already on an earlier track, and it fits horizontally. A net placed on this track blocks its VCG successors until the next track.

Example: spans net 1 [2, 7], net 2 [2, 6], net 3 [5, 8], net 4 [5, 7] and net 5 [3, 6] all overlap at columns 5 and 6, so five tracks are needed in any case, and the VCG only decides their top-to-bottom order. The algorithm is fast, $O(n \log n)$ plus the constraint checks, and it is guaranteed to finish whenever the VCG is acyclic, but it can use more tracks than the best routing.

## The top track and its limits

Only nets with no VCG predecessor can go on the top track, so the first pass is the unconstrained greedy restricted to those nets. Example: if nets 4 and 1 are the only predecessor-free nets and their spans do not overlap, the top track holds both.

The constrained greedy has two weaknesses. It ignores how long a net's chain of successors is, so it can delay a net that heads a long chain and waste tracks; refinements order candidates by chain length. And it fails outright on a cyclic VCG, where no net in the cycle is ever admitted. Doglegs, splitting a net's trunk at intermediate pins, fix both problems, and are the next step up.

## Going deeper

A. Hashimoto and J. Stevens (1971); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), on channel routing.

label: Cyclic vertical constraints
lesson:
# Cyclic vertical constraints

If net a must be above net b in one column and b above a in another, the vertical constraint graph has a cycle and no assignment of one trunk per net can satisfy both. Detecting cycles, and knowing how many nets must be split to break them, is the decision a channel router makes before it can place a single trunk.

## Detecting cycles

A net lies on a directed cycle of the VCG exactly when it can reach itself: run a search from each net, or compute strongly connected components and take every component with more than one net. If any net lies on a cycle, a dogleg-free channel routing is impossible, because the nets of the cycle would each have to be strictly above the next.

Example: top pins 3, 1, 5, 5 and bottom pins 5, 3, 4, 4 give edges $3 \to 5$, $1 \to 3$ and $5 \to 4$; if some column also gives $5 \to 1$ or $4 \to 3$, a cycle appears. Counting the nets on cycles tells you how much of the channel is affected.

## How many nets must be split

Splitting a net into subnets (a dogleg) can break a cycle, but only cycles that pass through a split net. So the set of nets a router splits must meet every cycle: it is a feedback vertex set of the VCG. The size of the smallest feedback vertex set is therefore a lower bound on the number of nets to split.

Example: a VCG whose cycles all pass through net 5 needs only one split. Finding a minimum feedback vertex set is NP-hard in general, but channel VCGs are small enough to search. The bound is not a guarantee: a split helps only if the net has a pin column between the two conflicting columns, where the dogleg can jump tracks.

## Shortest cycles

The shortest directed cycle tells you how tight the conflict is. A 2-cycle arises when two nets swap top and bottom positions in two columns, the most common case. Breadth-first search from each net for a path back to itself finds the shortest cycle in $O(V(V + E))$.

A short cycle between two nets whose pin columns interleave is easy to break with one dogleg. A long cycle through many nets suggests a pin arrangement that will cost several doglegs and extra tracks. Historically, channels with unbreakable cycles required changing the pin order or adding a column; in modern area routing the same situation shows up as a local knot of pins that only a reroute through another layer resolves.

## Going deeper

Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation", on channel routing with cyclic constraints; D. N. Deutsch, "A Dogleg Channel Router" (1976).

label: Dogleg channel routing
prereqs: Channel routing by the left-edge algorithm
lesson:
# Dogleg channel routing

A dogleg breaks a net's trunk into pieces at its intermediate pin columns, letting each piece sit on a different track. Deutsch's dogleg router (1976) applies this systematically: split every multipin net into two-pin subnets and route the subnets with the constrained left-edge algorithm. Doglegs break many vertical-constraint cycles and shorten constraint chains, usually saving tracks.

## Splitting into subnets

A net with pins in $m$ distinct columns $c_1 < \dots < c_m$ becomes $m - 1$ subnets with spans $[c_1, c_2], [c_2, c_3], \dots$. Adjacent subnets of one net meet at a pin column, where a vertical branch can join them even if they are on different tracks.

Example: nets with 2, 3, 3, 2 and 3 distinct pin columns become $1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8$ subnets. Two-pin nets are unchanged. The split happens only at pin columns, which is the restricted dogleg of Deutsch's algorithm; unrestricted doglegs may jog at any column but enlarge the search.

## The subnet VCG

Vertical constraints move to subnets. At a column with net $a$ on top and net $b$ at the bottom, only the subnets of $a$ and of $b$ that cover that column are constrained, with an edge from each such subnet of $a$ to each such subnet of $b$. Subnets of a net that do not reach the column are free of the constraint.

Example: if net 3 must be above net 2 at column 4 and net 2 above net 1 at column 9, but net 2's subnet at column 4 is not the one at column 9, the chain $3 \to 2 \to 1$ falls apart into two shorter chains. A path in the subnet VCG maps to a path in the net VCG, so splitting can never lengthen the longest chain.

## What doglegs buy

The longest-chain lower bound drops when splitting separates constraints that hit different parts of a net. Example: a net VCG whose longest chain has 3 nets may have a subnet VCG whose longest chain has 2, saving a track. Splitting also breaks many cycles, so the constrained left-edge algorithm can finish where it would otherwise fail.

Doglegs cost vias (each jog between tracks is a pair of vias in a two-layer channel) and leave cycles through two-pin nets untouched. Density is unaffected: doglegs do not change how many nets cross a column. So the dogleg router narrows the gap between the chain bound and density, but cannot go below density.

## Going deeper

D. N. Deutsch, "A Dogleg Channel Router" (1976); Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation".

label: Switchbox routing
lesson:
# Switchbox routing

A switchbox is a routing region with fixed pins on all four sides, typically where channels meet. Unlike a channel, it cannot grow tracks to fit its nets, so routability is a real question. Switchbox routing introduced the iterative, rip-up-based style of local routing that modern detailed routers use inside each clip.

## Channels versus switchboxes

A channel has pins on its top and bottom edges and open left and right ends; its height can grow until every net fits, so a channel router always succeeds by adding tracks. A switchbox has pins on all four sides, and its dimensions are fixed by its neighbours. Both bounds still apply: the nets crossing any vertical or horizontal cut line cannot exceed the tracks crossing it.

Example: a switchbox with 6 tracks and 7 nets crossing one vertical cut is unroutable as given, and no detailed router can fix that. Building-block layouts produced switchboxes at channel intersections, which is where they got their name.

## Routing inside a fixed box

Because constraints come from all sides, a single greedy pass rarely succeeds, so switchbox routers are iterative. They route the most constrained nets first, such as nets running straight across from one side to the opposite, then fit the rest, and rip up and reroute when a net is blocked. In a two-layer gridded box with one layer per direction, every bend is a via.

Density bounds are necessary but not sufficient: a box can respect every cut and still be unroutable because of how pins interleave. That is why switchbox routers report failure rather than adding tracks, and why the surrounding flow must be ready to change the box or its neighbours.

## Switchboxes in modern routers

Over-the-cell routing on many metal layers removed explicit channels from standard-cell designs, but the switchbox formulation survives. A detailed router's local repair works on a clip with its boundary connections fixed, which is exactly a switchbox, and the panels of track assignment are channels in all but name.

So a designer reads switchbox ideas as the logic of local repair: freeze the boundary, reroute inside, and accept that some local knots require changing the boundary (a larger clip or a different global route). FPGA routing has its own switch boxes, a programmable interconnect structure; the name is shared but the problem differs.

## Going deeper

Sherwani, "Algorithms for VLSI Physical Design Automation", on switchbox routing; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.).

label: Timing-driven routing
prereqs: Decomposing multipin nets into two-pin nets
Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Timing-driven routing

For most nets the router minimises wirelength, but for timing-critical nets the shape of the routing tree decides delay. A Steiner tree that shares a long trunk between sinks is short in total but slows the critical sink with capacitance it does not need. Timing-driven routing evaluates topologies by delay, usually Elmore delay, and picks the one that serves the critical sink best.

## Elmore delay through a shared trunk

Model the net as a tree of distributed RC wires: resistance $r$ and capacitance $c$ per micron, a driver of resistance $R_d$ and pin capacitances at the sinks. The Elmore delay to a sink is $R_d C_{total}$ plus, for every wire segment on the path to the sink, $r l (c l / 2 + C_{below})$, where $C_{below}$ is all capacitance downstream of that segment.

In topology A a trunk of length $l_0$ runs to a Steiner point and branches of length $l_1$ and $l_2$ go to sinks 1 and 2. The trunk sees everything below it: $C_{below} = c(l_1 + l_2) + C_1 + C_2$. Example: $R_d = 350$ ohm, $r = 1$ ohm/um, $c = 0.2$ fF/um, $l_0 = l_1 = 150$ um, $l_2 = 250$ um, $C_1 = 10$ fF and $C_2 = 5$ fF give a delay to sink 1 of 64 ps.

## Delay with separate wires

In topology B the driver feeds two separate wires, of length $l_0 + l_1$ to sink 1 and $l_0 + l_2$ to sink 2. The path lengths are the same as in A, but now sink 1's wire carries only its own capacitance: the delay is $R_d C_{total} + r d_1 (c d_1 / 2 + C_1)$ with $d_1 = l_0 + l_1$.

B uses more wire, $l_0$ extra, so the driver term grows. Whether B is faster for sink 1 depends on the balance: a strong driver (small $R_d$) with resistive wire favours B, because isolating sink 1 from sink 2's branch matters more than the extra load on the driver; a weak driver favours A. Real routers compare such topologies with Elmore or a better delay model and keep the one that meets the required time.

## Choosing by criticality

Timing-driven routing chooses topology per net by slack. Nets with ample slack get the shortest tree, because wirelength is what loads the routing grid and the driver. Nets with negative or small slack get trees that shorten the path to their critical sinks, even at a wirelength cost: shorter source-sink paths, critical sinks moved closer to the driver in the tree, or wider and higher-layer wires.

Example: a router that picks the topology with the smaller delay to sink 1 might choose B at 56.9 ps over A at 63.7 ps. The same reasoning drives net weighting in timing-driven placement and the Prim-Dijkstra trade-off for tree construction; the router's job is to apply it where the timer says it matters.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), on timing closure; J. Cong, A. B. Kahng and K.-S. Leung, "Efficient Algorithms for the Minimum Shortest Path Steiner Arborescence Problem" (1998).

label: Prim-Dijkstra routing trees
prereqs: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
lesson:
# Prim-Dijkstra routing trees

A minimum spanning tree minimises total wirelength; a shortest-path tree gives every sink the shortest path from the source. Timing-driven routing wants something in between. The Prim-Dijkstra construction of Alpert, Hu, Huang and Kahng blends the two with one parameter, trading wirelength for source-to-sink path length.

## Prim's end: c equals zero

Grow a tree from the source. At each step, over every tree pin $u$ and outside pin $v$, add the edge minimising $c \cdot pl(u) + d(u, v)$, where $pl(u)$ is the tree path length from the source to $u$ and $d$ is the Manhattan distance. With $c = 0$ the key is the edge length alone: this is Prim's algorithm, and the result is a rectilinear minimum spanning tree.

Example: source (8, 4) and sinks (7, 0), (0, 7), (1, 2) give an MST of length 19. Its radius, the longest source-to-sink tree path, can be long, because the MST happily chains sinks one after another away from the source.

## Dijkstra's end: c equals one

With $c = 1$ the key is $pl(u) + d(u, v)$, the length of the source path the new pin would get. This is Dijkstra's algorithm, and the result is a shortest-path tree: every sink's tree path equals the best achievable through the pins, so on a Manhattan plane the radius is minimal.

The price is wirelength. Each sink tends to connect almost directly toward the source, so sinks close to each other do not share wire. Example: a net whose MST is 44 might have a shortest-path tree of 79. Neither extreme is right for a critical net with many sinks: the MST is too slow, and the shortest-path tree loads the driver with too much capacitance.

## The trade-off in between

For $0 < c < 1$ the construction interpolates. Raising $c$ penalises attaching a sink to a tree pin that is already far from the source, so radius falls and wirelength rises; lowering it does the opposite. Example: with $c = 0.75$, a net might keep the MST's wirelength 36 and radius 19 if its sinks are already well placed, while other nets change shape sharply.

In practice tools pick $c$ per net from its criticality, then refine the tree into a Steiner tree and buffer it. The construction is $O(n^2)$ for $n$ pins, trivial next to routing, so it can be rerun whenever slack changes. A later refinement (PD-II) post-processes the tree to recover wirelength without lengthening critical paths.

## Going deeper

C. J. Alpert, T. C. Hu, J. H. Huang and A. B. Kahng, "A Direct Combination of the Prim and Dijkstra Constructions for Improved Performance-Driven Global Routing" (1993); C. J. Alpert et al., "Prim-Dijkstra Revisited" (2018).

label: Crosstalk-aware routing
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Crosstalk-aware routing

Wires on adjacent tracks are coupled through their sidewall capacitance. When a neighbour switches, it injects charge into the victim, changing its delay and possibly causing a glitch. At advanced nodes coupling is a large share of total wire capacitance, so routers control it by spacing, shielding and ordering wires, and timers model its effect on delay.

## Coupling capacitance

To first order, the coupling capacitance between two parallel wires grows with their parallel run length and falls with their spacing: $C_c \approx c_0 L s_0 / s$, where $c_0$ is the coupling per micron at the minimum spacing $s_0$. Real extraction uses tables or field solvers, and the dependence on spacing is weaker than $1/s$ once fringing dominates, but the trend is what a router uses.

Example: $c_0 = 0.05$ fF/um over a 1100 um parallel run at minimum spacing gives 55 fF of coupling, likely more than the victim's ground capacitance. Long parallel runs on adjacent tracks are therefore the crosstalk hazard routers look for.

## Miller factors and the delay window

The effect of $C_c$ on the victim depends on what the aggressor does. If it is quiet, $C_c$ acts like a capacitor to ground (Miller factor 1). If it switches in the same direction, the voltage across $C_c$ does not change and it disappears (factor 0). If it switches in the opposite direction, the voltage change doubles (factor 2). So the victim's effective load ranges from $C_g$ to $C_g + 2C_c$.

With a simple driver model, delay = $R_d C_{eff}$, so the delay varies by $R_d \cdot 2C_c$ between the best and worst case. Example: 160 fF of coupling behind a 250 ohm driver gives a window of $250 \cdot 320$ fF = 80 ps. Timers apply these factors per aggressor, using timing windows to decide which aggressors can switch together.

## Spacing and shielding

A crosstalk-aware router reduces coupling on critical nets. Spacing a victim one extra track away roughly halves $C_c$ in the first-order model, cutting the worst-case delay by $R_d \cdot 2 \cdot \Delta C_c$. Example: moving from 3 to 6 times minimum spacing over 2000 um with $c_0 = 0.06$ fF/um halves $C_c$ from 40 to 20 fF, saving $600 \cdot 2 \cdot 20$ fF = 24 ps behind a 600 ohm driver.

Shielding goes further: a grounded wire on the neighbouring track never switches, so it fixes the Miller factor at 1 and blocks the aggressor entirely, at the cost of a track. Routers also limit parallel run length between known aggressor and victim pairs, order nets within a panel so that nets with overlapping switching windows are not neighbours, and use non-default rules with double spacing for clocks.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), on timing closure.

label: Antenna-aware routing
lesson:
# Antenna-aware routing

During fabrication, metal is patterned one layer at a time with plasma etching, which deposits charge on exposed conductors. A long wire connected to a transistor gate, with no path to a diffusion yet, can collect enough charge to damage the thin gate oxide. Antenna rules limit the ratio of such metal to gate area, and routers must obey them or insert fixes.

## The partial antenna ratio

When layer $M_i$ is etched, the pieces of $M_i$ that are connected to a gate but not yet to any diffusion collect charge. The partial antenna ratio for $M_i$ is the area of that metal divided by the total gate area it connects to. (Rule decks may use top area or sidewall area, depending on the layer.)

Example: a net driving three gates of width 0.3 um and length 0.1 um has gate area 0.09 um$^2$. A gate-connected metal-2 piece 180 um long and 0.05 um wide has area 9 um$^2$, so the partial ratio is 100. The connection to diffusion usually comes through a driver's output, which may be reached only on a higher layer, so lower-layer pieces are exposed while they are etched.

## The longest legal wire

A rule caps the partial ratio at $R_{max}$ on each layer. For a wire of width $w$ attached to gate area $A_g$, the longest legal gate-connected length on that layer is $L_{max} = R_{max} A_g / w$. Example: $R_{max} = 700$, three gates of 0.2 um by 0.05 um (0.03 um$^2$) and a 0.1 um wire give $L_{max} = 210$ um.

The router can avoid violations by construction: when a net's route from its driver to a gate is long on a lower layer, it can climb to a higher layer near the gate. That piece on the lower layer is then disconnected from the gate while the lower layer is etched, and is connected only when the upper layer is built. This layer hop is called a jumper. Alternatively a reverse-biased diode near the gate gives the charge a path to the substrate.

## Cumulative ratios

Some rules use a cumulative antenna ratio: the sum of the partial ratios of all layers up to the current one. This captures charge collected over several etch steps. Example: gate-connected pieces of 20, 75 and 65 um on metals 1 to 3, all 0.05 um wide, connected to 0.1 um$^2$ of gate, give a cumulative ratio of $8 / 0.1 = 80$ at metal 3.

Antenna-aware routing handles this during search, by pricing long lower-layer runs toward gates, and afterwards, with a repair step that inserts jumpers or diodes on violating nets. OpenROAD includes an antenna checker and can repair violations by inserting diodes. Fixes cost something: jumpers add vias, diodes add capacitance and area.

## Going deeper

The LEF reference on ANTENNA properties (ANTENNAAREARATIO and ANTENNACUMAREARATIO); the OpenROAD documentation for antenna checking and repair.

label: Router core versus change surface
prereqs: Core versus change surface per engine
lesson:
# Router core versus change surface

An agent that customises a router must know which parts it may change freely and which it must never touch. The four-layer engine model gives the split: an immutable core that guarantees legal output, strategies that decide how to search, parameters that tune them, and hooks that expose live state. For a router, legality is the core and almost everything a customer asks for is surface.

## The four layers of a router

The core of a router is its DRC-correct path model and grid and layer legality: what geometry is allowed, how shorts and spacing are checked, how vias connect layers. Changing it needs human approval and full regression. The strategy layer holds the cost functions, the rip-up and reroute policy, net ordering and the search algorithm, selected from a library or added as plug-ins. Parameters are numbers such as via cost, history increment, present-factor growth, layer adjustments and iteration limits. Observation hooks expose the congestion map, violation markers and per-net state to an agent.

Example: an agent reading the congestion map after every global-routing iteration uses a hook; changing the history increment is a parameter; adding a new rip-up policy is a strategy plug-in; allowing off-grid wires is a core change.

## Why legality stays in the core

If each cost plug-in had to check shorts and spacing, one buggy plug-in could make the router emit an unmanufacturable layout. So legality is enforced by the core regardless of which strategy is active, and the seams between core and strategy carry contracts the core can enforce: costs must be finite and non-negative (search optimality depends on it), deterministic for the same inputs, and computed only from the context the seam passes.

The seam must expose enough context to make useful policies possible: the edge, its layer and direction, demand, capacity and history, the net and its criticality. A seam that hides criticality cannot host a timing-aware cost; one that exposes the whole database as text invites plug-ins that depend on internals and break when the core changes.

## Performance and determinism at the seam

Router kernels are hot loops: a maze search expands millions of states. A plug-in called through a virtual function per edge expansion can slow the search several times and stop the compiler from optimising it. Seams should therefore be coarse: a plug-in computes a cost map per region or per iteration, which the kernel reads as a table.

Plug-ins must also be deterministic with no hidden global state, so the same design routes the same way twice; otherwise golden and differential tests are meaningless. A customer preference such as making vias near an analog block ten times more expensive is a strategy or parameter change, not a core edit. A change to what geometry is legal is the rare core change, and is treated as one.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD drt and grt source structure as a case study.

label: Cost functions as router plug-ins
lesson:
# Cost functions as router plug-ins

The router's cost function is its most customer-specific behaviour: every team wants to penalise something different, from vias on critical nets to wiring over an analog block. Making the cost a plug-in at a defined seam lets an agent add or modify it as a Tier 2 change, while the core keeps search and legality fixed. The design question is what the seam passes and promises.

## Evaluating a plug-in cost

A cost plug-in receives an edge's context and returns a price. Example: $cost(e) = b_e(1 + \alpha\max(0, d_e + 1 - c_e)^2) + \beta h_e$, plus $\gamma$ for every via on a timing-critical net. With $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = 4$, a via edge with demand 5 and capacity 4 and history 3 costs $1 \cdot (1 + 4) + 3 + 4 = 12$, while a free wire edge with history 0 costs 1.

The core sums plug-in costs along each candidate and keeps the cheapest path, exactly as with a built-in cost. Squaring overflow is a typical Tier 2 idea: heavily overflowed edges become much more expensive, so demand spreads more aggressively at some cost in wirelength. The plug-in changes prices only; it cannot make an illegal path legal.

## The seam contract

For the core to trust a plug-in, the seam states a contract: finite, non-negative costs; deterministic results for the same context; no hidden global state; and only the context the seam passes. The core checks what it can, rejecting or clamping negative costs, because Dijkstra and A* lose optimality with them.

Performance is part of the contract. A plug-in that precomputes a cost map per iteration lets the maze kernel read a table instead of calling out per edge, which keeps the hot loop tight. The context the seam passes defines what is possible: to discourage vias on critical nets, the seam must expose whether an edge is a via and the net's slack or criticality.

## Proving a plug-in correct

A plug-in is accepted on evidence, not on reading its code. A differential run on reference designs, with and without it, must show that only the targeted nets' routes moved, that DRC stayed clean, and that global metrics (overflow, wirelength, timing) moved as intended. A plug-in that reduces overflow but raises detailed-routing violations is optimising a proxy that ignores something the next stage cares about.

When the same request recurs with different numbers, for example a different overflow exponent per design, the knob belongs in configuration: expose it as a plug-in parameter so the request becomes Tier 1. That is how the change surface grows deliberately, and how a validated plug-in eventually becomes a library skill.

problems.q:
A team registers a Tier 2 edge-cost plug-in in a router's cost seam: $cost(e) = b_e(1 + 2\max(0,\ d_e + 1 - c_e)^2) + 0 h_e$, plus 2 for every via on a timing-critical net. The router core calls it for each edge it expands and keeps its own legality checks. All edges have $b_e = 1$, and the net being routed is timing-critical. Candidate paths: path A: via (demand 0, cap 2, history 0), wire (demand 1, cap 3, history 0), via (demand 3, cap 3, history 0), wire (demand 1, cap 2, history 1); path B: wire (demand 2, cap 3, history 3), wire (demand 3, cap 3, history 2); path C: wire (demand 3, cap 3, history 0), wire (demand 3, cap 4, history 3), wire (demand 2, cap 3, history 3). Which path does the router choose?

A) Path B

B) Path A

C) No path: the plug-in must first reject the overflowed edges

D) Path C

label: Layer directives as Tier 1 changes
lesson:
# Layer directives as Tier 1 changes

Many routing requests are about layers: route this block only on M2 to M6, keep clocks above M5, reserve capacity on M2 for pin access, give these nets double width. These are layer directives, and a well-designed router makes them Tier 1 configuration that the core already enforces. An agent should never write code for them, but it must still verify their consequences.

## Directives as configuration

A layer directive restricts or reshapes the resources the router may use, through settings the core already understands. Minimum and maximum routing layers bound the whole design. Per-net-class layer ranges restrict, for example, clock nets to M5 and above. Layer adjustments reduce a layer's capacity by a percentage. Non-default rules assign wider wires and larger spacing to named nets. Routing blockages forbid layers over a region.

Each is a typed setting, validated when it is read and enforced by the core as legality. That makes them Tier 1: no recompile, no new code, and the same behaviour every time the setting is used. OpenROAD, for instance, exposes routing layer ranges and per-layer adjustments as commands in its flow scripts.

## Tier 1 versus Tier 2

A request is Tier 1 when an existing setting expresses it. Forbid routing below M7 over an analog region: a set of routing blockages, Tier 1. Make vias on timing-critical nets more expensive only when slack is below a threshold: a conditional cost that no setting expresses, so it needs a cost plug-in, Tier 2. Allow wires off the track grid: a change to legality, Tier 3.

Directives must be validated, not silently ignored. A net restricted to M2 through M4 whose pin sits only on M6 cannot be routed; the router must report the conflict rather than drop the pin or quietly use M6. Common, well-defined requests belong in Tier 1 precisely because a typed setting is safer and faster than new code, and because an agent can check it mechanically.

## Directives still need verification

Configuration changes behaviour. Lowering the maximum routing layer from M8 to M6 removes all capacity on M7 and M8, so overflow and detours rise and long critical nets lose their low-resistance layers. Restricting all nets to M2 and M3 removes most of the stack's capacity and will overflow heavily. So an agent applying a directive still runs the golden designs: DRC-clean, overflow within limits, timing within tolerance.

Recurring Tier 2 requests are a signal to grow Tier 1. If teams keep asking for different via costs per layer, the engine should expose a per-layer via-cost table. Legality on the chosen layers, direction, spacing and via rules, remains the core's job whatever the directive says.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD grt documentation for routing layers and layer adjustments.

problems.q:
A user asks that a block be routed only on M2 through M6. Which change tier is this?

A) Tier 2: write a layer plug-in

B) Tier 1: set the minimum and maximum routing layers

C) It requires a new PDK

D) Tier 3: change the core grid model
problems.a: Tier 1: set the minimum and maximum routing layers
problems.e: Routing-layer limits are standard configuration directives that the core already honours.

problems.q:
A user asks that a block be routed only on M2 through M6. Which change tier is this?

A) It requires a new PDK

B) Tier 2: write a layer plug-in

C) Tier 1: set the minimum and maximum routing layers

D) Tier 3: change the core grid model
problems.a: Tier 1: set the minimum and maximum routing layers
problems.e: Routing-layer limits are standard configuration directives that the core already honours.

problems.q:
A team reduces the usable capacity of M2 by 30% to leave room for pin access. Which tier is this?

A) A change to the cell library

B) Tier 1: a layer capacity adjustment

C) Tier 2: a new congestion model

D) Tier 3: a change to legality
problems.a: Tier 1: a layer capacity adjustment
problems.e: Layer adjustments are parameters that scale gcell capacities.

problems.q:
A customer wants vias on timing-critical nets to cost more only when the net's slack is below a threshold. Which tier is this?

A) Tier 3: a core edit to via legality

B) Tier 1: set the maximum routing layer

C) Tier 1: change the global via cost

D) Tier 2: a cost plug-in that reads net slack
problems.a: Tier 2: a cost plug-in that reads net slack
problems.e: A conditional cost needs code at the cost seam, but no legality change.

problems.q:
A user asks to forbid routing over a sensitive analog region on all layers below M7. Which is the most appropriate tier?

A) Tier 3: change the grid model

B) Tier 1: routing blockages for those layers over the region

C) Ask the placer to move the region

D) Tier 2: a new search algorithm
problems.a: Tier 1: routing blockages for those layers over the region
problems.e: Region and layer blockages are configuration that the core already enforces as legality.

problems.q:
Why should layer directives be Tier 1 rather than written as plug-ins each time?

A) Plug-ins cannot read layers

B) They are common, well defined and checkable, so a typed setting is safer and faster than new code

C) Layer choice is part of the core legality

D) Tier 1 changes need recompilation
problems.a: They are common, well defined and checkable, so a typed setting is safer and faster than new code
problems.e: Frequent, simple requests belong in configuration so that an agent never needs to edit code for them.

problems.q:
An agent proposes a Tier 1 directive that restricts all nets to M2 and M3. What is the likely outcome?

A) Heavy overflow, because two layers cannot carry the demand that the full stack carried

B) Better timing on every net

C) No change, since directives are advisory

D) Fewer vias and no other effect
problems.a: Heavy overflow, because two layers cannot carry the demand that the full stack carried
problems.e: Capacity is the sum over layers; removing most layers removes most capacity.

problems.q:
An agent changes the maximum routing layer from M8 to M6 to save mask cost. What must it check before promoting the change?

A) Nothing, since Tier 1 changes cannot break anything

B) Only that the setting parses

C) Only that runtime dropped

D) That the golden designs still route DRC-clean and that overflow and timing stay within tolerance
problems.a: That the golden designs still route DRC-clean and that overflow and timing stay within tolerance
problems.e: Configuration changes behaviour; fewer layers can cause overflow or timing loss, so the golden and QoR checks still apply.

problems.q:
Which part of a layer directive must remain enforced by the core rather than by the directive itself?

A) How much each layer costs

B) The order of nets

C) Which layers the user prefers

D) That wires on each layer obey its direction, spacing and via rules
problems.a: That wires on each layer obey its direction, spacing and via rules
problems.e: Directives restrict choice; legality on the chosen layers remains the core's responsibility.

label: DRC-clean as the router's golden test
lesson:
# DRC-clean as the router's golden test

A router change is accepted only if routed reference designs come out clean. DRC-clean, connected and within a quality-of-results tolerance is the router's golden test, and a differential comparison against the baseline proves the change touched only what it was meant to. These checks are what let an agent edit routing policy at all.

## Wirelength against the baseline

Each golden design has a stored baseline routing. A new build must route it with zero DRC violations and zero opens, the hard gates, and then its quality metrics are compared with the baseline: wirelength, via count, overflow, timing. The wirelength change is $(WL_{new} - WL_{base}) / WL_{base} \times 100\%$.

Example: a baseline of 264972 um and a new result of 265025 um is a change of 0.02%. Hard gates come first: a shorter routing with one short is a failure, not an improvement. Tolerances are needed because routers are heuristic, but they must be tight enough to catch real regressions.

## Differential checks

A golden test asks whether the result is good; a differential test asks whether it changed only where intended. Route the reference design with and without the change and compare per net. Example: a plug-in meant to affect clock nets only must leave every signal net's route identical. If two signal nets changed wirelength, the check fails, even if total wirelength improved.

Unintended changes reveal one of two problems: the seam leaks behaviour outside its scope (the plug-in's cost touched edges used by other nets), or the router is not deterministic. Both must be fixed before promotion, because otherwise nobody can tell whether later differences come from the change or from noise.

## The golden suite

One design is not enough: a suite covers dense and sparse regions, macros, many layers and few, different rule decks. A change is promoted only when every design passes every gate. Example: with a 1% wirelength tolerance, results of +2.7%, -1.9%, -2.2%, +0.5% with two opens, and +0.5% clean fail four of five designs.

For an agent this suite is the reward signal, and it must be hard to game. Checking DRC with the router's own fast checker invites changes that satisfy the checker but not the signoff engine; skipping connectivity invites deleting wires to remove violations. Golden criteria therefore use the signoff DRC engine, an independent connectivity check and timing, and they are versioned together with the baselines.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD regression test suite as an example.

problems.q: A router change is checked on a golden reference design. The baseline routing has 518853 um of wirelength; the new build routes it DRC-clean with 533142 um. What is the wirelength change, in percent of the baseline? Round to 2 decimal places (negative means shorter).
problems.e: (533142 - 518853) / 518853 x 100 = 2.75%. A QoR gate compares this against a tolerance only after the hard gates, zero DRC violations and zero opens, have passed.
