label: Agentic DRC-repair loops
prereqs: DRC-clean as the router's golden test
lesson:
# Agentic DRC-repair loops

After detailed routing, a few hundred violations often remain, clustered around crowded cells and macros. An agentic repair loop reads the DRC report, proposes local fixes, runs them through the router, verifies, and iterates, with a human approving the final change. It is the routing instance of an agentic signoff or ECO loop, and its value depends on what it is allowed to change and how it checks itself.

## Read, propose, verify

Each iteration starts from the router's DRC report: violation types, layers, locations and the nets involved. The agent proposes a fix within its allowed change surface, such as ripping up and rerouting the nets in a window around a cluster with a higher marker penalty, enlarging a clip, changing a net's layer range, or adding a non-default rule. The router executes the fix, and the agent verifies the repaired region and the whole design: no new violations, no opens, no new timing failures.

When the count falls and then oscillates, say between 3 and 5, the current move is not converging. The loop must escalate: widen the window, change strategy, or hand the residue to a human, instead of repeating the same move.

## Rewards that cannot be gamed

An agent optimising violation count will find shortcuts if they exist. Editing the rule deck to relax spacing removes violations without fixing anything; the deck is fixed by the foundry and outside the agent's surface. Deleting a net's last segment removes a violation and leaves an open; a connectivity check catches it. Satisfying the router's fast internal checker but not the signoff engine is reward hacking against a proxy.

So the reward combines signoff DRC on the final layout, a connectivity check and timing, and the loop runs in a sandbox with versioned, reversible changes. Design data stays inside the IP boundary; only the know-how, what kind of fix worked, may leave it.

## From repeated fixes to skills

Repairs work on windows, not on the whole design, because local changes are cheaper to verify and less likely to disturb nets that were already clean, and because the resulting diff is reviewable. When the same move repeatedly fixes the same kind of violation across designs, say an end-of-line pattern next to a particular cell, it is a candidate skill: validate it with golden and differential tests and promote it into the router's library of repair strategies.

A human still approves the final routing ECO, reviewing the diff and the check results. The loop's job is to do the tedious search and to present evidence; it does not sign off its own work. Fixes that trade one failure for another, such as removing violations while degrading slack, must be rejected by the acceptance check.

problems.q:
What does an agentic DRC-repair loop read at each step?

A) Only the total wirelength

B) The placement density map only

C) The router's DRC report: violation types, layers, locations and the nets involved

D) The RTL source
problems.a: The router's DRC report: violation types, layers, locations and the nets involved
problems.e: Repair needs to know what failed and where; the violation report is the observation.

problems.q:
Which action is an appropriate first proposal for a cluster of spacing violations around one pin-dense cell?

A) Rerun synthesis

B) Rip up and reroute the nets in a window around the cell with a higher marker penalty

C) Change the foundry spacing rule

D) Delete the cell from the netlist
problems.a: Rip up and reroute the nets in a window around the cell with a higher marker penalty
problems.e: Local rip-up with stronger penalties is the standard repair move; rules and netlist are outside the router's authority.

problems.q:
What does an agentic DRC-repair loop read at each step?

A) The RTL source

B) The router's DRC report: violation types, layers, locations and the nets involved

C) Only the total wirelength

D) The placement density map only
problems.a: The router's DRC report: violation types, layers, locations and the nets involved
problems.e: Repair needs to know what failed and where; the violation report is the observation.

problems.q:
Which reward is hardest to game for a DRC-repair agent?

A) Violations reported by the signoff DRC engine on the final layout, together with opens and connectivity checks

B) The agent's confidence score

C) Violations reported by the router's own fast checker

D) The number of nets the agent touched
problems.a: Violations reported by the signoff DRC engine on the final layout, together with opens and connectivity checks
problems.e: The signoff checker is the ground truth; a fast internal checker is a proxy that an agent can learn to satisfy without real fixes.

problems.q:
An agent proposes to fix violations by relaxing a spacing value in the rule deck. What is wrong?

A) Nothing, it removes the violations

B) The rule deck is fixed by the foundry; fixing the layout by editing the checker hides real defects

C) Spacing values do not matter

D) Rule decks are Tier 1 configuration
problems.a: The rule deck is fixed by the foundry; fixing the layout by editing the checker hides real defects
problems.e: This is reward hacking: the metric improves but manufacturability does not. Rules are outside the agent's change surface.

problems.q:
Why should repair proposals be sandboxed and reversible?

A) Sandboxes make the router faster

B) A bad fix must be undone without corrupting the design database, and nothing may leak outside the IP boundary

C) Reversibility is required by the PDK

D) It lets the agent skip DRC checks
problems.a: A bad fix must be undone without corrupting the design database, and nothing may leak outside the IP boundary
problems.e: Changes run in isolation with versioned results so failures are cheap and design data stays on-site.

problems.q:
A repair loop has fixed similar end-of-line violations on many designs with the same move. What does the skill flywheel suggest?

A) Validate the move with golden and differential tests and promote it into a library repair strategy

B) Hard-code it into the core

C) Keep it in the agent's prompt only

D) Discard it after each design
problems.a: Validate the move with golden and differential tests and promote it into a library repair strategy
problems.e: A repeated successful fix becomes a compiled, reusable skill once it passes validation.

problems.q:
Who approves the final routing ECO produced by an agentic repair loop?

A) The fast congestion estimator

B) A human, reviewing the diff and the check results

C) The agent itself

D) Nobody, once DRC is clean
problems.a: A human, reviewing the diff and the check results
problems.e: Agentic loops propose and verify; signoff of the final change stays with a human.

problems.q:
A repair loop has fixed similar end-of-line violations on many designs with the same move. What does the skill flywheel suggest?

A) Hard-code it into the core

B) Discard it after each design

C) Keep it in the agent's prompt only

D) Validate the move with golden and differential tests and promote it into a library repair strategy
problems.a: Validate the move with golden and differential tests and promote it into a library repair strategy
problems.e: A repeated successful fix becomes a compiled, reusable skill once it passes validation.

label: Fast congestion estimators in modeling loops
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast congestion estimators in modeling loops

An agent exploring placement and flow options cannot afford a full global route for every candidate. It needs a fast congestion estimator in its loop and a rule for when to trust it and when to call the accurate router. RUDY and probabilistic estimators are the classic fast modes; knowing what they miss is what makes the loop safe.

## The RUDY estimate

RUDY (rectangular uniform wire density, Spindler and Johannes) spreads each net's expected wire uniformly over its bounding box. For a box $W$ by $H$ and wire pitch $p$, the half-perimeter wire occupies area $p(W + H)$, so the density inside the box is $p(W + H)/(WH)$, the fraction of the box's area taken by the net.

Example: pitch 0.2 um and a 31 by 35 um box give $0.2 \cdot 66 / 1085 = 0.012$. Small boxes are dense, long thin boxes spread thin. RUDY needs no routing and no decomposition, and it changes smoothly when cells move, so a placer can evaluate it, and even differentiate it, inside its own optimisation loop.

## Summing over a tile

The demand map adds the RUDY densities of every net whose box covers a tile. Example: two nets whose boxes contain a 1 by 1 um tile with densities 0.035 and 0.032 give the tile a density of 0.067, and nets whose boxes miss it contribute nothing. Comparing the map with the routing capacity per tile flags likely hot spots.

The estimate is cheap because it ignores everything a router does: it assumes wire spreads evenly over the box, ignores detours, blockages and layer limits, and treats multipin nets as their half-perimeter. It is good at ranking regions and poor at absolute overflow, which is why it serves as a fast mode, not as signoff.

## When to recurse to the accurate router

In a modeling loop the agent flags a tile for the accurate global router only when the fast estimate exceeds a threshold. The dangerous errors are misses: tiles the estimator called safe that the accurate router later finds overflowed. Counting them on calibration designs sets the threshold. Example: if several tiles with fast utilisation below 0.8 overflow under the accurate router, the threshold must drop or the estimator must improve.

The loop should also recurse when the estimate's variance is high, when a candidate is about to be committed, and periodically to recalibrate. This is the fast-versus-accurate pattern of agent-first engines: cheap models explore, accurate engines decide, and the agent watches the disagreement between them as closely as it watches either one.
